14	# Two Studies Issurin Cites Against Simultaneous Development: Swimmer Interference and Kayaker Decay
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents two data-backed examples as motivation for abandoning
17	simultaneous multi-ability training (traditional periodization) in favor of consecutive,
18	concentrated blocks.
19	
20	**(1) Swimmer concurrent-training interference (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp. 10-11, Figure
21	1.3).** High-level male swimmers were studied over an 8-week early-season program combining
22	extensive swimming with resistive/power dry-land work aimed at swim-specific strength
23	(9-11 workouts/week; sample size not stated in this text). Measured: maximal force of
24	tethered swimming (Ftsw), dry-land explosive strength (Fexp), and dry-land strength
25	endurance (SE). Result: strength endurance improved markedly; swim-specific strength did not
26	improve; explosive strength *decreased* — despite about 30% of dry-land program time devoted
27	to maximal/explosive strength work. Issurin's mechanistic explanation: extensive endurance
28	work captures the metabolic (anabolic) energy needed for the hypertrophy and neural-drive
29	adaptations that explosive/maximal strength require, and the resulting chronic fatigue keeps
30	central and peripheral neural factors from the state needed for strength gains
31	(citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point).
32	
33	**(2) Kayaker decay under traditional periodization (PDF p. 25-26, printed pp. 14-15,
34	Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
35	the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
36	of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
37	model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
38	threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
39	long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
40	during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic work and
41	maximum-strength work were reduced or dropped as "harmful for racing technique," and V-AT,
42	peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive period. Distance velocity
43	still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
44	reduced force — i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
45	aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
46	was far from optimal."
47	
48	**Why it works** — For the swimmer case, Issurin's own stated mechanism is that extensive
49	endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is necessary for anabolism during
50	post-exercise recovery," suppressing the muscle hypertrophy and neural-drive adaptations
51	strength training requires, and that chronic fatigue from high-volume training keeps
52	"central and peripheral neural factors... far from optimum" (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp.
53	10-11, citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point). For the kayaker case, Issurin
54	gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
55	aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14) — treat
56	that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
57	cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
58	categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
59	offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
60	non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
61	motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
62	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
63	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].
64	
65	**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
66	controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
67	useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
68	programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
69	many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
70	mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
71	letting it decay unaddressed."
72	
73	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
74	this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
75	from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
76	`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the
77	original 1986/whichever-year source Issurin drew Figure 1.3 from (not cited by name on this
78	page). **Untested:** the kayaker case is Issurin's own team's data (Issurin et al., 1986),
79	observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
80	not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
81	athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
82	competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
83	the kayakers' single annual peak design.
84	
85	**Example** — A Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
86	strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
87	failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
88	load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
89	programmed.
90	
91	**Related** — [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (Table 1.4's rationale,
92	which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
93	[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

Figure 1.4 — the in-text citation reads "Fig.1.3," which appears to be a labeling error in
the source; the described variables match Figure 1.4's caption, not Figure 1.3's).** A group
of highly qualified kayakers were tracked across a full annual cycle built on the classical
model (Issurin et al., 1986). Measured: mean distance velocity (Vd), velocity at anaerobic
threshold (V-AT), peak paddle force (PF), stroke rate (SR), muscle mass (MM). Result: the
long general-preparatory period raised V-AT, muscle mass and peak force substantially; but
during the extended, highly specialized competitive period, extensive aerobic work and
maximum-strength work were reduced or dropped as "harmful for racing technique," and V-AT,
peak force, and muscle mass all *declined* by the competitive period. Distance velocity
still reached its season maximum, but only via increased stroke rate compensating for
reduced force — i.e., technique/rate covered for a real loss in the underlying strength and
aerobic qualities. Issurin's summary: "the timing pattern for developing different abilities
was far from optimal."

endurance work "captures the metabolic energy that is necessary for anabolism during
post-exercise recovery," suppressing the muscle hypertrophy and neural-drive adaptations
strength training requires, and that chronic fatigue from high-volume training keeps
"central and peripheral neural factors... far from optimum" (PDF pp. 21-22, printed pp.
10-11, citing Klausen, 1990, for the neural-mechanism point). For the kayaker case, Issurin
gives no physiological mechanism for the decline beyond narration of what happened (reduced
aerobic and strength work during the competitive period, PDF p. 25, printed p. 14) — treat
that case as a described pattern, not an explained one. **Inference:** labeling the two
cases as "concurrent interference" versus "sequential decay" is this entry's own
categorization for cross-referencing purposes, not language Issurin himself uses; both are
offered by Issurin as evidence for the same underlying argument against simultaneous,
non-block training (see [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), which in turn
motivates the consecutive block sequencing in
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]] and
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]].

**When to apply** — The swimmer study is the stronger evidence of the two: it is a
controlled, measured 8-week study with named outcome variables, giving concrete numbers
useful for illustrating concurrent-training interference to Baylor strength staff
programming for athletes who need both an aerobic base and explosive/max strength (e.g.,
many football positions in a fall-camp conditioning window). The kayaker case is useful
mainly as a cautionary illustration of "building a quality early in the year and then
letting it decay unaddressed."

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The swimmer study's exact sample size is not given in
this text (only workout frequency, 9-11/week), so its statistical strength cannot be judged
from this source alone — treat the direction of the finding (interference occurred) as
`supported` but the specific numeric changes in Figure 1.3 as unverifiable without the

observational across one season with no control group — it demonstrates a plausible pattern,
not a controlled comparison against an alternative periodization model run on the same
athletes. Neither study is football-specific; football's in-season structure (weekly
competition, not one late-season peak) differs from both the swimmers' fixed 8-week block and
the kayakers' single annual peak design.

**Example** — A Baylor position group with both an in-season conditioning demand and a
strength-maintenance demand should treat "just add more of both" as the swimmer study's
failure mode: without deliberate sequencing or volume management, the concurrent aerobic
load can blunt the intended strength/power adaptation even when strength work is
programmed.

which these two studies are offered as concrete illustrations of),
[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]].

14	# Squat-First vs. Squat-After-Hang-Pull Changes Whether You Get More Reps or More Power
15	
16	**What it is** — Spreuwenberg et al. (2006), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62):
17	**nine** resistance-trained male athletes performed the back squat (4 sets at 85% of 1RM) on
18	two separate days under two protocols. Protocol A: squat performed during the initial part
19	of the workout. Protocol B: squat performed after a whole-body resistance exercise (hang
20	pull). Results: Protocol A produced significantly more repetitions per set (8.0 ± 1.9 vs.
21	5.4 ± 2.7 in Protocol B), but average power per set was *higher* in Protocol B. Issurin
22	attributes the power difference to postactivation potentiation induced by the preceding
23	whole-body power exercise.
24	
25	**Why it works** — Issurin reports only the study authors' own attribution for the power
26	finding: they "attributed this phenomenon to postactivation potentiation induced by the
27	preceding whole-body power exercise" (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62). **Inference:** the
28	companion explanation for the rep-count finding, that fresh (unfatigued) muscle sustains
29	more total repetitions at a given relative load than muscle that has just performed a
30	preceding whole-body lift, is this entry's own reasoning to account for the Protocol A
31	result; Issurin does not state that explanation for the rep-count difference in this
32	passage.
33	
34	**When to apply** — Choosing exercise order based on the specific training goal for that
35	session: Issurin's stated takeaway (PDF p. 73, printed p. 62) is that a coach wanting maximum
36	hypertrophy stimulus should place the squat early in the session (more total volume/reps),
37	while a coach targeting maximum power output should place it after appropriate whole-body
38	resistance work, to exploit postactivation potentiation. Directly usable for Baylor
39	strength-staff session design when max-effort lower-body power output (not volume) is the
40	stated goal of a given lift.
41	
42	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a small (n = 9), single published study;
43	Issurin does not report effect sizes, statistical significance values, or the specific
44	whole-body exercise's loading in this citation beyond "hang pull" — treat the direction of
45	the finding as `supported` but do not treat the exact magnitude (8.0 vs. 5.4 reps) as
46	something to replicate precisely without reading the original study. It is unclear from this
47	text whether the postactivation-potentiation effect generalizes to different athlete
48	populations (this sample was resistance-trained males), different preceding exercises, or
49	different rest intervals between the potentiating exercise and the squat.
50	
51	**Example** — A power-focused lower-body day for football linemen might sequence a
52	moderate-load hang pull or clean pull before back squats at 85% 1RM, accepting fewer total
53	squat reps in exchange for higher power output per rep on the squats that follow — a
54	hypertrophy-focused day for the same lift would instead put the squat first.
55	
56	**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
57	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].
58

14	# A Structured Warm-Up/Cool-Down Program Cut Soccer Injuries Roughly Four-Fold Over Six Months
15	
16	**What it is** — Ekstrand et al. (1983), cited by Issurin (PDF p. 58, printed p. 47,
17	Figure 2.1): **twelve** national-division soccer teams (**180 players**) were split into two
18	groups. The intervention group (six teams) used a modified program with carefully structured
19	warm-ups (ball exercises plus a stretching program) and cool-downs (jogging plus hold-relax
20	stretching), supervised by doctors and physiotherapists. The control group (six teams)
21	trained traditionally. Over a six-month follow-up, the intervention group showed "highly
22	significant superiority": a roughly **four-fold reduction in the number of injuries** and a
23	"drastic decrease" in workouts and games missed to musculoskeletal disorders. Issurin
24	separately cites supporting single-factor findings: stretching in warm-up increases lower
25	extremity range of motion in soccer players (Moller et al., 1985); active warm-up *without*
26	stretching does not affect flexibility (Zakas et al., 2006); and intense prior exercise
27	meaningfully stimulates aerobic metabolism in working muscles during subsequent strenuous
28	performance (Bangsbo et al., 2001). A related study (Moller et al., 1985, PDF p. 68, printed
29	p. 57) tracked 48 adult soccer players across three warm-up/cool-down protocols and found
30	that inserting a stretching series into the *cool-down* (not just the warm-up) produced range-
31	of-motion benefits both immediately after the session and 24 hours later, while stretching
32	only in the warm-up helped immediately but not at 24 hours.
33	
34	**Why it works** — Issurin frames warm-up and cool-down as serving three functions each:
35	metabolic adjustment, technical/coordination adjustment, and mental readiness (warm-up,
36	Table 2.6, PDF p. 60, printed p. 49); and reduction of body temperature/HR/blood pressure,
37	removal of metabolic byproducts, endocrine-system recovery, and reduced emotional tension
38	(cool-down, Table 2.11, PDF p. 69, printed p. 58). **Contested — flag directly:** Issurin's
39	cool-down rationale explicitly frames blood lactate and "other acid metabolites" as "waste
40	products" to be "removed" from the muscles (PDF p. 68-69, printed pp. 57-58), citing a
41	specific clearance kinetic (blood lactate removal after a 4-minute exhausting time trial
42	takes about 20 minutes, Juel et al., 1990). This is in tension with a modern-physiology
43	claim already captured in this library's Verkhoshansky staging
44	([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]], `proven`): lactate is
45	not a toxin causing soreness or requiring active "removal," and it clears from the blood on
46	its own within about an hour of strenuous exercise regardless of cool-down activity, with
47	current research attributing post-exercise soreness to muscle/connective-tissue microtrauma
48	rather than residual lactate. The specific clearance-time citation (20 minutes for a 4-minute
49	time trial) may still be a real kinetic fact — that is not itself disputed here — but
50	Issurin's *framing* of this as evidence that cool-down actively "removes" a harmful waste
51	product reflects the outdated "lactic acid as toxin" model the Verkhoshansky entry corrects.
52	Cite this book's clearance-time number without repeating its waste-product framing.
53	
54	**When to apply** — The Ekstrand et al. (1983) result is directly relevant to Applied
55	Performance's collaboration with Athletic Medicine on injury reduction: a structured,
56	medically-supervised warm-up/cool-down protocol is associated with a large, measured
57	reduction in soft-tissue injury incidence in a team sport, over a real six-month season, not
58	an acute lab measure. The cool-down-stretching timing finding (Moller et al., 1985) suggests
59	cool-down, not just warm-up, is where a stretching series may do more for next-day range of
60	motion.
61	
62	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is an observational, non-randomized team-level
63	comparison (teams chose or were assigned to conditions; individual randomization is not
64	described), and the intervention bundled multiple changes at once (warm-up content, cool-down
65	content, and medical/physiotherapy supervision), so the four-fold injury reduction cannot be
66	attributed to warm-up or cool-down alone — Issurin himself flags this study as "atypical
67	because it refers to the complex effects of warming-up, cooling-down and medical supervision"
68	(PDF p. 58, printed p. 47). **Contested:** stretching's effect on preventing delayed-onset
69	muscle soreness specifically is described by Issurin himself as disputed within this same
70	chapter — "supported by several studies (Hartfield, 1985) and contradicted by others (High
71	et al., 1989)" (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59) — do not cite stretching-prevents-DOMS as settled.
72	
73	**Example** — A Baylor position group's practice-ending routine that pairs light locomotion
74	with a stretching series (rather than stretching only in the pre-practice warm-up) has some
75	support here for next-day range-of-motion benefit, though the causal strength of the
76	underlying Moller et al. (1985) study for injury outcomes specifically (as opposed to ROM)
77	is not established by this citation.
78	
79	**Related** — [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--lactate-and-oxygen-debt-myths]] (staging;
80	the direct source of the lactate-framing contest above — recommend the Verkhoshansky entry
81	add a reciprocal link back to this one once both are reviewed).

14	# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once
15	
16	**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
17	modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
18	**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
19	long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
20	19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
21	peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
22	23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
23	within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm) across a combined **155-day** span (winter ~20
24	days; spring/summer 135 days), 14-25 day intervals. Issurin's summary point: these athletes'
25	5-8 month competitive spans "can not be subdivided into traditional preparatory and
26	competitive periods," yet their basic abilities (max strength, aerobic regeneration
27	capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire span.
28	
29	**Why it works — this is observational, not interventional** — These are real competition
30	records for three specific, historically documented elite athletes (Olympic/World
31	champions), not an experiment; the "why" is a report of what elite competition calendars
32	actually looked like by 1991/1998, cited to Suslov's (2001) analysis rather than derived
33	from a controlled study of periodization models.
34	
35	**When to apply** — As direct evidence for the strength-and-conditioning miss-log's
36	"peaking phase structure" gap: this table is the empirical case Issurin uses to argue that a
37	single annual peak (or even a two-/three-peak model) does not describe how modern elite
38	individual-sport athletes actually compete, which motivates the multi-stage annual model in
39	[[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]]. Useful for framing the *problem*
40	(competition calendars now demand many peaks) to Baylor coaches even before the
41	*solution* (Chapter 3's microcycle-level guidance, not yet ingested) is available.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — All three examples are individual, non-contact,
44	technique/power sports (sprinting/jumping, pole vault, high jump) where "peak" can be defined
45	by a single measurable performance (time, height, distance) on a given day. **Inference:**
46	this evidence does not directly transfer to football, where "peak" is not a single
47	measurable output and the competitive calendar is fixed by a weekly game schedule rather
48	than a chosen sequence of meets — the multi-peak *problem* generalizes (a football season
49	also demands repeated high-level performance, not one), but the specific 19-43 day
50	inter-peak intervals shown here are specific to how often these particular athletes chose to
51	compete, not a transferable spacing rule for football practice or game weeks. Data source is
52	single (Suslov, 2001, "with modifications" by Issurin) with no stated method for how "peak"
53	was defined or verified for each performance.
54	
55	**Example** — When explaining to a Baylor position group why in-season programming assumes
56	more than one readiness peak per season, this table is a citable, real-world existence proof
57	that elite athletes routinely peak 7-11 times in a season — useful for framing, not for
58	directly copying an inter-peak interval into a football in-season plan.
59	
60	**Related** — [[framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]].

15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin extends the BPC concentration principle (see
17	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]) down to the level of a single session.
18	A **key-workout** is the most important development session in a training cycle, focused on
19	the current main training emphasis (Table 2.5, PDF p. 56, printed p. 45): it targets the
20	cycle's most relevant abilities (usually one motor-fitness and one technique/tactics
21	target), demands focused athlete motivation and coach support, is timed for the athlete's
22	"best time" (adjusted to prior load but not overly fatigued), is loaded at a
23	substantial/large/extreme level, favors partnership/team-spirit organizational forms, and
24	requires thorough objective monitoring (chronometry, HR, blood lactate, video). New,
25	unfamiliar training means should *not* be introduced during a key-workout, since novelty
26	diverts attention and motivation from load-specific execution. Within a workout, the
27	analogous concept is the **key-exercise** (or **key-task** in team/combat sports where a
28	scrimmage or sparring session plays the role) — the single most important exercise, given
29	priority placement, maximal self-motivation and support, "prime-time" timing, and careful
30	monitoring (Table 2.9, PDF p. 64, printed p. 53). Issurin gives typical prescriptive ranges
31	for key-exercises by targeted ability (Table 2.10, PDF p. 67, printed p. 55, based on Fox &
32	Mathews 1981 and Viru 1995, "with author's modification"): maximal speed, 7-15s work at a
33	1:10 work/rest ratio, maximal intensity, 5-8 reps, 2-5 series; anaerobic glycolytic power,
34	30-50s, 1:(4-5), submaximal, 4-6 reps, 2-4 series, blood lactate >8 mmol/L and HR >180;
35	anaerobic glycolytic endurance, 1-1.5 min, 1:3, high intensity, 8-12 reps, 1-3 series,
36	maximal lactate >8 and HR >180; aerobic power, 1-2 min, 1:(1-0.5), intermediate, 5-8 reps,

38	4-16 reps, 1-3 series, lactate 2.5-4(5) and HR 140-160; restoration/fat oxidation, 20-90 min,
39	low intensity, 1-3 reps, HR 100-140.

42	viewpoint of block training, the emphasis on key-function exercises/drills is very
43	characteristic. Following the principle of training workload concentration (1.2.2) the

14	# Structuring Two-a-Day (and Denser) Training Days by Dominant Ability and Rest Interval
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin describes how high-performance programs structure multiple same-day
17	sessions, most commonly two-a-days but up to four (routine in training-camp practice) or
18	occasionally six (an "exception," per anecdotal coach reports, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65). For
19	a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77, printed p. 66): session 1
20	(early morning) uses small load — warm-up, alactic bouts combined with medium-intensity
21	aerobic work, addressing morning stiffness/soreness; session 2 (mid-morning, after a
22	multi-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — aerobic interval series combined with
23	technical tasks, where sprint bouts interact positively with the aerobic work; session 3
24	(early afternoon, after a one-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — concentrated aerobic
25	work; session 4 (late afternoon, after a three-hour break) uses substantial load — continuous
26	aerobic exercise and aerobic-resistance work, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given
27	accumulated fatigue. For anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67):
28	session 2 uses substantial load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt
29	accumulation); the one-hour break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated
30	lactate to be oxidized (Volkov, 1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work
31	still starts with an already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a
32	three-hour break, athletes arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance,

# Structuring Two-a-Day (and Denser) Training Days by Dominant Ability and Rest Interval

**What it is** — Issurin describes how high-performance programs structure multiple same-day
sessions, most commonly two-a-days but up to four (routine in training-camp practice) or
occasionally six (an "exception," per anecdotal coach reports, PDF p. 76, printed p. 65). For
a four-session aerobic-development day (Figure 2.5, PDF p. 77, printed p. 66): session 1
(early morning) uses small load — warm-up, alactic bouts combined with medium-intensity
aerobic work, addressing morning stiffness/soreness; session 2 (mid-morning, after a
multi-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — aerobic interval series combined with
technical tasks, where sprint bouts interact positively with the aerobic work; session 3
(early afternoon, after a one-hour break) uses medium/substantial load — concentrated aerobic
work; session 4 (late afternoon, after a three-hour break) uses substantial load — continuous
aerobic exercise and aerobic-resistance work, with an emphasized, longer cool-down given
accumulated fatigue. For anaerobic-development days (Figure 2.6, PDF p. 78, printed p. 67):
session 2 uses substantial load for anaerobic glycolytic power (fast lactate/oxygen-debt
accumulation); the one-hour break before session 3 allows roughly 70-80% of accumulated
lactate to be oxidized (Volkov, 1986), so session 3's anaerobic glycolytic capacity work
still starts with an already-activated glycolytic/enzymatic system; session 4 (after a
three-hour break, athletes arriving fatigued) targets anaerobic strength endurance,
deliberately sustaining progressive fatigue. For the more common two-a-day structure, Table
2.13 (PDF p. 79, printed p. 68) gives compatible first/second-workout pairings by dominant
ability: aerobic power/capacity — fartlek (10-15s sprint, 3-6min at anaerobic threshold)
first, aerobic interval series second; anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity — anaerobic power
interval series first, anaerobic capacity interval series second; maximal speed — anaerobic
alactic interval series first, anaerobic alactic plus explosive strength exercises second;
techno-tactical abilities — techno-tactical simulation/maximum speed first, match/scrimmage
second.

session's fatigue and metabolic byproduct load has cleared before the next session begins,
and the daily plan deliberately exploits this: shorter breaks (one hour) leave residual
glycolytic activation that *helps* a subsequent glycolytic-capacity session, while longer
breaks (three hours) still leave athletes fatigued enough that only fatigue-tolerant
modalities (strength endurance, continuous aerobic work) are appropriate for the day's final
session.

**When to apply** — Directly applicable to football fall-camp scheduling, where two-a-day
sessions are standard. **Eric's baseline** names a specific priority stack for fall camp —
"Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39) — and Table 2.13's
maximal-speed pairing (anaerobic alactic interval series both sessions, explosive strength
added to the second) is a directly relevant template for structuring a two-a-day built
around that same alactic/aerobic priority.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin gives no controlled-study citation for the
specific figures in this section (session load levels, the four-session structure, the
70-80% lactate-oxidation-in-one-hour figure attributed to Volkov, 1986, is the one sourced
number; the rest of the daily-series structure reads as the author's own applied synthesis).

individual/endurance-and-power sports generally); the specific break lengths (one hour,
three hours) and load progressions should be treated as a template to adapt, not a
prescription to copy directly into a football fall-camp schedule without accounting for
football-specific factors (equipment, heat, practice structure, position-group differences)
not addressed in this chapter.

**Example** — A fall-camp two-a-day built around the department's stated alactic/aerobic
priority could pair a morning session of alactic interval sprint work with an afternoon
session combining more alactic work and explosive strength (per Table 2.13's maximal-speed
row), rather than defaulting to a generic "conditioning AM, lift PM" split that does not
target a specific dominant ability across the two sessions.

14	# Which Training Modalities Tolerate Fatigue, and Which Need a Fresh Athlete
15	
16	**What it is** — Figure 2.3 (PDF p. 72, printed p. 60) ranks eleven training modalities by
17	how much athlete fatigue they can tolerate before the acute training effect is compromised,
18	from "well rested" through "slightly fatigued," "moderately fatigued," to "fatigued":
19	**require well-rested or only slightly fatigued athletes** — maximal speed (least
20	fatigue-tolerant of all), acquisition of new technical skills, explosive strength, maximal
21	strength (neural mechanism, e.g. 1-3RM); **tolerate up to moderate fatigue** — anaerobic
22	glycolytic power, technique perfection, aerobic power, maximal strength (hypertrophy, e.g.
23	8-10RM); **tolerate fatigue through to the end of the session (most fatigue-tolerant)** —
24	anaerobic glycolytic capacity/endurance, aerobic endurance (long duration), strength
25	endurance, flexibility. Issurin's stated reasoning (PDF pp. 71-73, printed pp. 60-62):
26	exercises needing precise excitatory neural output (max speed, explosive strength, technical
27	skill acquisition, neural-mechanism strength) are blocked by inhibitory CNS output in
28	fatigued athletes, so they belong early; anaerobic glycolytic power needs available energy
29	reserves that are depleted in fatigued athletes; hypertrophy-strength work depends on total
30	mechanical work and post-exercise recovery conditions (not the athlete's pre-exercise
31	freshness), so it can be placed later or even after an endurance session; anaerobic
32	glycolytic capacity and strength/aerobic endurance work are defined by sustained effort
33	*despite* accumulating fatigue, so some fatigue is expected and even required for the
34	intended stimulus.
35	
36	**Why it works** — CNS-dependent, high-precision, high-velocity qualities are limited by
37	inhibitory neural output and available energy stores that both degrade with fatigue,
38	while volume/duration-dependent qualities (hypertrophy, strength/aerobic endurance) depend
39	on total accumulated work or post-session recovery rather than the athlete's moment-to-moment
40	freshness — so sequencing exists to protect the fatigue-sensitive qualities' window, not
41	because "harder exercises always go first."
42	
43	**When to apply** — Ordering exercises within a single practice or lift: place max-speed
44	work, new skill acquisition, explosive strength, and low-rep neural-strength work at the
45	start of a session (or after only light warm-up fatigue); place hypertrophy work, technical
46	perfection under fatigue, and long-duration aerobic/strength-endurance work later, when some
47	accumulated fatigue is acceptable or even intended. Issurin gives a worked example (PDF
48	p. 72, printed p. 61): an endurance athlete needing to preserve muscle mass can have a
49	hypertrophy-focused strength session (8-10RM) placed *after* a medium-load endurance
50	session, because hypertrophy's driver is total mechanical work and post-workout recovery
51	conditions, not pre-workout freshness — this would be the wrong sequencing choice for a
52	neural-strength (1-3RM) session, which does need "prime time."
53	
54	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no primary citation for Figure 2.3
55	itself** — it reads as the author's own synthesized ranking rather than a reproduced,
56	independently-sourced scale; treat the ordinal ranking (which modality is more or less
57	fatigue-tolerant than its neighbor) as a reasonable but unvalidated synthesis, not a measured
58	result. The figure gives no guidance on *how much* fatigue is "slight" vs. "moderate" in
59	objective terms (RPE, HR, or specific fatigue markers), so applying it requires a coach's own
60	judgment call about where an athlete currently sits on that continuum. It also does not
61	address multi-session days directly — see [[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]]
62	for cross-session sequencing.
63	
64	**Example** — A football practice combining new install (technical skill acquisition) with
65	conditioning: install work belongs at the start of practice when players are fresh and can
66	attend to technical detail; conditioning work belongs at the end, where sustained effort
67	under fatigue is the intended stimulus rather than a limitation.
68	
69	**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
70	[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].
71

14	# Quantifying Workout Load on a 1-5 Scale, Mapped to Borg RPE Bands
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin presents a load-related workout classification built around three
17	functions: **development**, **retention**, and **restoration** (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41).
18	Table 2.3 (PDF p. 53, printed p. 42, based on Zatsiorsky 1995, modified by Issurin 2003)
19	quantifies this on a 1-5 scale using restoration time as the objective marker: restoration
20	level 1 (< 12 hours), retention level 2 (12-24 hours), development-substantial level 3
21	(24-48 hours), development-large level 4 (48-72 hours), development-extreme level 5
22	(> 72 hours). Because restoration-time-based classification does not fit every training type
23	well (Issurin notes coordination/neuro-emotional-stress workouts need less restoration time
24	than the scale implies), Table 2.4 (PDF p. 54, printed p. 43) offers a parallel mapping using
25	Borg's Rate of Perceived Exertion scale (Borg, 1973): RPE 6-11 (very-very-easy to
26	fairly-easy) = restoration; RPE 12-14 (slightly difficult) = retention; RPE 15-16
27	(difficult) = development-substantial; RPE 17-18 (very difficult) = development-large; RPE
28	19-20 (very-very difficult) = development-extreme.
29	
30	**Why it works — inference on the underlying logic** — Restoration time and perceived
31	exertion are both proxies for how disruptive a session was to homeostasis; using either (or
32	both together) lets a coach assign every workout a comparable numeric load value even in
33	non-measurable sports (team sports, gymnastics), which Issurin identifies as the practical
34	payoff: "the load level of each workout can be quantified and expressed numerically" (PDF
35	p. 54, printed p. 43), enabling load-dependent categorization (development vs. retention vs.
36	restoration) across an entire training plan, not just isolated hard/easy labeling.
37	
38	**When to apply** — Building a simple, athlete-reportable RPE-based load log for sports or
39	settings where objective physiological monitoring (HR, blood lactate) is not available for
40	every session; classifying a completed week of training after the fact into
41	development/retention/restoration proportions to check whether the intended block emphasis
42	(see [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]) was actually
43	delivered. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name Borg's RPE scale specifically, though
44	session-level subjective load tracking is philosophically consistent with the department's
45	general preference for practical, staff-sustainable monitoring tools over burdensome ones
46	(`method-baseline.md`, "Load monitoring and GPS," on why daily wellness surveys were
47	abandoned when athletes learned to game them) — RPE has its own well-documented gaming risk
48	that is not addressed anywhere in this Issurin chapter and should be treated as an open
49	question, not assumed solved.
50	
51	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — **The author gives no mechanism** for why these
52	specific RPE cut-points (11/12, 14/15, 16/17, 18/19) map to these specific restoration-time
53	bands rather than some other set of cut-points; both tables are presented as ready-made
54	scales without a validation study cited in this chapter. RPE is a subjective, athlete-reported
55	measure and is vulnerable to the same reporting-fatigue and gaming dynamics documented
56	elsewhere for subjective wellness tools; do not treat it as equivalent in reliability to the
57	objective HR/blood-lactate markers used in Table 2.10's key-exercise prescriptions
58	(see [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]). The scale also does not
59	distinguish RPE driven by physical load from RPE driven by psychological/technical/cognitive
60	demand (e.g., a technically difficult but physically light session), a limitation Issurin
61	himself flags when noting coordination-heavy sessions need less restoration than their
62	subjective difficulty might imply.
63	
64	**Example** — A coach without force-plate or HR-monitor access for every practice can have
65	players self-report session RPE, multiply by session duration (an approach not itself stated
66	in this chapter but a standard extension of Borg RPE elsewhere in sport science, noted here
67	as an inference, not something Issurin describes), and classify the week's development
68	vs. retention vs. restoration balance against the intended training-stage emphasis.
69	
70	**Related** — [[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]],
71	[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

13	
14	# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
17	foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
18	(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
19	"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
20	consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
21	abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
22	printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
23	traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
24	printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
25	physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
26	once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
27	fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
28	stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
29	among many abilities.
30	
31	**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
32	a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
33	threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
34	stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
35	threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
36	principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
37	than derived from a stated dose-response model.
38	
39	**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
40	more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
41	Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
42	"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
43	full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
44	citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
45	[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
46	describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.
47	
48	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
49	traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
50	preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
51	lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
52	concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal

# Concentration of Training Workloads Is the Cornerstone Principle of Block Periodization

**What it is** — Issurin states the Block Periodization Concept (BPC) rests on one
foundational principle, concentration of training workloads, from which two others follow:
(1) a minimal number of targeted abilities per block, because highly concentrated loads
"only provide sufficient training stimuli to improve the targeted ability," and (2)
consecutive (not simultaneous) development of abilities, because "the number of decisive
abilities exceeds the number of abilities that can be developed simultaneously" (PDF p. 37,
printed p. 26, Figure 1.7). The rationale is laid out as a table of contradictions in the
traditional, simultaneous-development model for high-level athletes (Table 1.4, PDF p. 20,
printed p. 9): concurrent workloads compete for limited energy supply, differing
physiological-system restoration times leave athletes under-recovered for all targets at
once, workloads interact negatively (energy deficits, technical complexity, neuromuscular
fatigue), mental concentration cannot be split across many targets, and the training
stimulus needed for a high-level athlete's progress cannot be reached when it is divided
among many abilities.

**Why it works** — Issurin's own explanation is that above a threshold of athletic level,
a quality only responds to a training stimulus concentrated enough to exceed that
threshold; splitting the same total training time across many qualities keeps each one's
stimulus below that threshold. He does not give a quantitative mechanism for where that
threshold sits or how "concentrated enough" is defined for a given ability or athlete — the
principle is argued from coaches' and scientists' collective experience (Table 1.4) rather
than derived from a stated dose-response model.

**When to apply** — Designing training blocks for advanced, high-level athletes juggling
more qualities than can be trained well at once (the explicit target population, per
Issurin). **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own compatibility rule,
"you can't ride two horses with one saddle" — incompatible qualities are not both trained at
full intensity in the same block (`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.28-29). It also converges with
[[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]], which independently
describes concentrated, saturated loading on one quality with a delayed 4-12 week rebound.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Issurin's own text (PDF p. 44, printed p. 33) states the
traditional, complex (simultaneous multi-ability) model "has visible benefits for the
preparation of low- and mid-level athletes": it is "more diversified, attractive and
lively," and medium-level concentration is "sufficient stimulation" at that level — the
concentration principle is explicitly scoped to high-performance athletes, not a universal
programming rule. **Contested:** Issurin's blanket claim elsewhere in the same chapter that
the traditional model "does not work well for high-performance athletes" (PDF p. 19,
printed p. 8) is disputed by this library's own Bompa & Haff 5th-edition material
(`periodization--bompa`), which is a current (not 1984-vintage) textbook still teaching and
defending a form of the traditional/complex periodization model for high-level athletes.
Issurin's critique in this chapter names Bompa's *1984* edition specifically (PDF p. 13,
printed p. 2) as one of the texts that propagated the traditional model he is arguing
against — it is not a critique of the Bompa & Haff 5th edition already in this library,
which incorporates concentrated-loading and conjugated-sequence ideas closer to Issurin's
own. **Inference:** Issurin's own later peer-reviewed review (2016, *Sports Medicine*,
"Benefits and Limitations of Block Periodized Training Approaches," Zotero item
`PT9QTQ2I`, not yet full-text-cached in this ingest) is titled around limitations as well as
benefits and likely narrows this 2008 book's confident framing; treat the frontmatter
`confidence: contested` as applying specifically to the universal "traditional doesn't work
for high performers" claim, not to the narrower, self-limited concentration principle.

**Example** — A collegiate football strength staff trying to develop max strength,
aerobic capacity, alactic power, and technical skill acquisition all at full intensity in
the same 4-week block, per Table 1.4's logic, risks under-stimulating all four rather than
meaningfully improving any one; concentrating the block on 1-2 of them (with the rest held
at a retention dose) is the alternative Issurin argues for.

**Related** — [[framework--block-periodization-mesocycle-taxonomy]] — the three-block
structure this principle produces. [[periodization--bompa/principle--concentrated-loading-overreaching]]
and [[periodization--bompa/framework--step-loading-paradigm]] — converging concentrated-load
ideas already in this library. [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]] (staging) —
check for overlap on why generalized simultaneous training under-delivers for advanced
athletes.

# Step Loading (the 3:1 Microcycle Paradigm)

**What it is** — The classic periodization loading model: training load rises in a *wavelike* pattern across microcycles rather than continuously. The canonical form is **3:1** — load increases across three microcycles (weeks), then drops in a fourth unloading week for regeneration before the next series begins. Variants scale to the athlete: **4:2** (four loading weeks, two unloading) for more advanced work, **2:1** for younger or less-trained athletes. Because a single session can't drive noticeable adaptation, the load is held across a microcycle, then stepped up.

**Why it works** — Loading accumulates fatigue across the three steps; the unloading week sheds fatigue, raises preparedness, and lets the supercompensation/adaptation surface before the next overload (see [[principle--supercompensation-cycle]], [[heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]). It operationalizes progressive overload safely (see [[principle--progressive-overload-threshold]]). The more progressive loading steps, the longer the unloading needed.

**When to apply** — Default structure for organizing weeks within a training block; choosing a loading ratio by training age; scheduling deloads on purpose rather than reactively.

**When NOT to apply** — Pure **linear loading** (continuous increase, no unloading) only works for short stretches — sustained, it causes overtraining, burnout, and injury. Classic step loading can also create **monotony** if every day of the microcycle repeats the same load; remedy with greater intra- and inter-microcycle variation, or use a **summated microcycle** (each week emphasizes a different quality — strength-endurance, max strength, speed-strength, restoration — reintroduced cyclically), better suited to intermediate/advanced athletes.

**Example** — A four-week block runs weeks 1–3 with rising volume/intensity and week 4 as a deload; a developing athlete instead runs a 2:1 pattern so recovery arrives sooner.

# The Two-Factor Model Can Be Formalized Mathematically, and Its Research Base Argues Against Heavy Training Right Before Competition

**What it is** — The Two-Factor (Fitness-Fatigue) Model treats preparedness at time t as
initial preparedness plus the summed effect of a slow-decaying fitness after-effect and a
faster-decaying fatigue after-effect, each with its own magnitude and decay-time constant
(Banister et al., 1992). Banister and Calvert (1980) originated this with the Training
Impulse (TRIMP), a quantified unit of training load used to model and predict elite
swimming performance from the fitness/fatigue balance. Zatsiorsky (1995) is cited for the
same 3:1 fitness-to-fatigue decay ratio already in this library's Bompa material. Later
research building on this model examined tapering specifically: Fitz-Clarke et al. (1991)
found presently accepted taper protocols may be too rigorous and short for best results,
and several studies (Zarkadas et al. 1995; Mujika et al. 1996; Shepley et al. 1992) found
that proper placement of training volume during a taper is a key optimization factor, with
high training volume in the days immediately preceding competition possibly detrimental to
performance. Different muscle groups recover heterochronically, which is why some Russian
restoration specialists deliberately avoid applying restorative methods (e.g. massage) to
every muscle group after every session, since supercompensation is reportedly more
pronounced with partial rather than total restoration. (PDF pp. 99-100, printed pp. 88-89.)

**Why it works** — Modeling preparedness as the sum of two exponentially-decaying
after-effects with different time constants gives periodization a quantitative structure
(not just a qualitative "wave" description), which is what allows taper researchers to ask
a specific, testable question: how much and how recently loaded should training be before
competition to maximize the fitness-minus-fatigue difference at competition time.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this is the more technical, equation-based underpinning
of this library's already-captured practical rule
([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]]); cite this entry when a
more rigorous or quantitative framing is needed (e.g. explaining the model to a sport
scientist or in a research-facing document), and cite the Bompa heuristic for the everyday
coaching rule of thumb. The taper-volume finding directly supports reducing training
volume, not just intensity, in the days immediately before a competition or key testing
date.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific mathematical constants (A, B, T1, T2)
must be fit per individual and per training phase, and the text notes they require
periodic re-estimation; do not treat this as a plug-and-play formula without that
fitting process. The taper studies cited are from the early-to-mid 1990s and largely from
swimming; **Inference:** don't assume the exact taper-volume findings transfer unchanged to
football or other team sports without independent verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** rather than assuming a flat "taper week" cuts intensity but
keeps volume similar, this model's logic and the cited taper research both point toward
deliberately reducing volume (not just easing intensity) in the final days before a key
competition or test date, to let the longer-lasting fitness effect show through as the
shorter fatigue effect clears.

**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]],
[[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]].

85	As can be seen in Table 3.1 the microcycles differ in purpose, load level, 
86	design, particulars, and duration. For example, the adjustment microcycle at the 
87	beginning of the season usually lasts a whole week. In the middle of the season this 
88	microcycle can be planned at the beginning of a new stage or used to start a training 
89	camp. In both cases its duration can be shorter (3-5 days) and depends on the 
90	circumstances of preparation. Note that gradual increases in load level relate not only 
91	to physiological demands (i.e. magnitude of training stimuli) but also to the mental 
92	load component. This can be particularly important in the training camp, where 
93	athletes simultaneously receive new cognitive and emotional demands. Similarly, the 
94	restoration microcycle varies in duration depending on fatigue level and the demands 
95	of preparation. Usually in mid-season, the restoration microcycle after training camp 
96	and/or after competition lasts 3-4 days. 
97	  
98	
99	===== PDF PAGE 89 =====
100	
101	78 
102	 
103	The loading microcycles encompass mostly routine work and usually last one 
104	week but, this duration is not firmly set. Load administration in this cycle is 
105	considered separately in the next section. The impact microcycle focuses on maximal 
106	loads and can last less than a week. Special requirements should be in place to supply 
107	restorative means that are necessary for such microcycles in order to fulfill their goals. 
108	Proper diet, nutritional supplements, hydrotherapy, massage, mental relaxation, etc. 
109	can be parts of the special restoration program.  
110	 
111	A pre-competitive microcycle can be shorter or longer than a week. It 
112	normally has two purposes: to provide mental, physical and techno-tactical tuning for 
113	a forthcoming event, and to provide full (or sometimes partial) recovery of athletes 
114	after serious loads. Consequently, this microcyle is characterized by a remarkable 
115	load reduction. The competitive microcycle is exclusively sport-specific; this 
116	determines its content, particulars and duration which, in extreme cases, can be more 
117	than one week, as in multi-day road cycling competitions. For instance, the world 
118	famous cycling “Tour-de-France” lasts twenty three days including two days off. 
119	Thus, this competition embraces three successive microcycles. The sequencing of 
120	different microcycles is considered in 3.2.  
121	 
122	3.1.2. Load variations within the microcycle (wave-shape design) 
123	 
124	It is commonly known that the load level should be varied within a 
125	microcycle. The main factors determining load variations are load summation that 
126	causes fatigue accumulation, and restoration, which is affected by the use of reduced 
127	load level workouts and other means of restoration. Previous considerations of load 
128	variability have been based on general categories such as small, medium and high 
129	load levels (Martin,1980; Starischka, 1988) or in percentages of maximum 
130	(Dick,1980; Platonov,1997; Bompa,1999). Adequate and integrative load description 
131	is a problem, particularly for non-measurable sports like sailing or team and dual 
132	sports. The 5-point load level scale presented in the previous chapter (2.1.3) makes it 
133	possible to formalize workload alterations within several microcycles. For example 
134	see typical load variations in microcycles having one workout per day in Figure 3.1.

137	to perform relatively large amounts of weekly workloads with reduced risk of

Chapter 3 
 
Microcycles, 
mesocycles  
and training stages 
 
 
 
 The microcycle  is the shortest training cycle. It encompasses a number of 
workouts and lasts a number of days, most often one week. The mesocycle, a 
medium size training cycle, incorporates a number of microcycles. A number of 
mesocycles in a specific sequence and with purposeful interaction form a 
training stage that is usually directed to competition. This chapter presents and 
elucidates the basics, essentials and designs of the various training units.  
 
 
3.1. Microcycles 
  
As stated above, the microcycle usually lasts one week. This uniformity has no 
physiological rationale but rather is based on social life; athletes combine training 
with education and professional activity, and their normal desire to spend weekends 
with family and friends. However, training camps make it possible to create shorter 
and longer microcycles.  These possibilities are considered below. Our attention in 
this chapter is directed to the types and specifications, load variations, compatibility 
of adjacent workouts, and in particular, the content of various microcycles. 


===== PDF PAGE 88 =====

77 
 
 
3.1.1. Types and specifications of microcycles  
 
 There are six types of training microcycles, chara cterized by specific purposes, 
load levels, particulars of workload design and duration (Table 3.1).

As can be seen in Table 3.1 the microcycles differ in purpose, load level, 
design, particulars, and duration. For example, the adjustment microcycle at the 
beginning of the season usually lasts a whole week. In the middle of the season this 
microcycle can be planned at the beginning of a new stage or used to start a training 
camp. In both cases its duration can be shorter (3-5 days) and depends on the 
circumstances of preparation. Note that gradual increases in load level relate not only 
to physiological demands (i.e. magnitude of training stimuli) but also to the mental 
load component. This can be particularly important in the training camp, where 
athletes simultaneously receive new cognitive and emotional demands. Similarly, the 
restoration microcycle varies in duration depending on fatigue level and the demands 
of preparation. Usually in mid-season, the restoration microcycle after training camp 
and/or after competition lasts 3-4 days. 
  

===== PDF PAGE 89 =====

78 
 
The loading microcycles encompass mostly routine work and usually last one 
week but, this duration is not firmly set. Load administration in this cycle is 
considered separately in the next section. The impact microcycle focuses on maximal 
loads and can last less than a week. Special requirements should be in place to supply 
restorative means that are necessary for such microcycles in order to fulfill their goals. 
Proper diet, nutritional supplements, hydrotherapy, massage, mental relaxation, etc. 
can be parts of the special restoration program.  
 
A pre-competitive microcycle can be shorter or longer than a week. It 
normally has two purposes: to provide mental, physical and techno-tactical tuning for 
a forthcoming event, and to provide full (or sometimes partial) recovery of athletes 
after serious loads. Consequently, this microcyle is characterized by a remarkable 
load reduction. The competitive microcycle is exclusively sport-specific; this 
determines its content, particulars and duration which, in extreme cases, can be more 
than one week, as in multi-day road cycling competitions. For instance, the world 
famous cycling “Tour-de-France” lasts twenty three days including two days off. 
Thus, this competition embraces three successive microcycles. The sequencing of 
different microcycles is considered in 3.2.  
 
3.1.2. Load variations within the microcycle (wave-shape design) 
 
It is commonly known that the load level should be varied within a 
microcycle. The main factors determining load variations are load summation that 
causes fatigue accumulation, and restoration, which is affected by the use of reduced 
load level workouts and other means of restoration. Previous considerations of load 
variability have been based on general categories such as small, medium and high 
load levels (Martin,1980; Starischka, 1988) or in percentages of maximum 
(Dick,1980; Platonov,1997; Bompa,1999). Adequate and integrative load description 
is a problem, particularly for non-measurable sports like sailing or team and dual 
sports. The 5-point load level scale presented in the previous chapter (2.1.3) makes it 
possible to formalize workload alterations within several microcycles. For example 
see typical load variations in microcycles having one workout per day in Figure 3.1.             
 
Three- and two-peak designs are used most widely because they allow athletes 
to perform relatively large amounts of weekly workloads with reduced risk of 

===== PDF PAGE 90 =====

79 
 
excessive fatigue accumulation. The two or three load reductions facilitate athletes’ 
restoration and stimulate their readiness to effectively perform subsequent high 
demand workouts. The key-workouts concentrate the most important workloads of 
dominant training modalities.

The one-peak design can be employed to concentrate a number of developing 
workouts in order to attain a more profound and stressful training response.  This 
result can be used as preparation for further medium- and low-level workouts in 
which several technical and/or tactical tasks can be accomplished with gradual 
recovery. Such concentration of one-peak development workouts can definitely be 
used by sufficiently prepared high-performance athletes but not by novice and less 
prepared athletes. 
 
When athletes do two or more workouts per day, the daily point-score is raised 
by each workout making the weekly point-score much higher (Figure 3.2). The graph 
displays load variations within a microcycle, where each coordinate summarizes the 
load values of one or two single workouts for several days. The load value for each 

===== PDF PAGE 91 =====

development workouts followed by two medium load supporting workouts.  This 
makes restoration possible prior to the second mini-block of workloads composed of 
three development sessions including two key-workouts. The last session on Saturday 
can be devoted to a time-trial or a match in team or dual sports, or in some other 
competitive simulation.

Additional remarks can be made about a quantification system based on a 5-
point scale. Its utilization offers a number of possible benefits. 
 
First, the graphic presentation of the workload, particularly in non-measurable 
sports, gives additional support for coaches to analyze the load level of each workout 
and to quantify it more accurately.  Also, different microcycles (one-, two- and, three-
peak designs) can be expressed numerically and presented in visual form. 
 
Second, the microcycle graph can be used didactically.  Athletes can relate 
more consciously to training demands since they can better appreciate the importance 
of key-workouts and anticipate restoration after the stressed load peaks. 

===== PDF PAGE 92 =====

81 
 
 
Third, the total point-score of the whole microcycle can be used for general 
load evaluation and for comparing different microcycles. In this manner, planning 
technology can be enhanced. 
 
As previously stated, the Block Periodization approach assumes a high 
concentration of specialized workloads directed at a minimum number of targeted 
abilities (1.3).  This in turn determines the special demands of the appropriate 
microcycles, which should show mostly separate, not complex, distribution of 
workloads taking into account their reciprocal interactions and expected training 
residuals.  
 
The next paragraphs consider the most widely used aerobic (or strength-
aerobic) microcycle (3.1.3), anaerobic glycolitic microcycle (3.1.4), microcycle for 
explosive strength in highly coordinated exercises (3.1.5), and the pre-competitive 
microcycle (3.1.6).

575	team and dual sports and combat sports) dictate involvement of short-duration bouts 
576	(alactic) and more prolonged efforts (glycolitic). In addition, the use of short-duration 
577	sprints makes it possible to diversify the training routine but without attempting to 
578	enhance maximal speed.

581	makes it more difficult to perform proper technique and techno-tactical skills.

583	performance. Hence, these skills should be properly enhanced with respect to extreme 
584	physical and emotional exertions, i.e. within the framework of highly intense 
585	workload microcycles.

900	effect also plays a decisive role in training responses to explosive strength sessions.  
901	Testosterone as the primary male sex hormone, determines the anabolic effect of 
902	strength training.  In addition, its variations during athletic training indicate the level 
903	of induced physical stress (Viru and Viru, 2000). For example, the influence of 
904	testosterone on explosive performance was examined in a special study (Cardinale 
905	and Stone, 2006) 
906	 
907	Case study . Seventy elite athletes in track and field (sprinters), handball, 
908	volleyball and soccer players (a total of 22 women and 48 men) participated. 
909	Resting testosterone levels in blood and height of a countermovement vertical 
910	jump were examined after 10 hours of fasting and one day of rest. A significant 
911	positive relationship was found between testosterone levels and jump performance 
912	(r = 0.61, p <0.001). Thus, testosterone levels strongly affect power output in 
913	muscular efforts having short contraction times (Cardinale and Stone, 2006). 
914	 
915	  
916	The study findings lead to at least two conclusions for explosive strength 
917	training: 
918	1)  persons with relatively high testosterone levels (both male and female athletes) 
919	have an inherited predisposition for explosive strength performance; 
920	2)  the training design in microcycles for explosive strength development should 
921	avoid excessive fatigue that suppresses the testosterone level and sharply 
922	reduces the effect of maximal power exercises.

927	(1.2.2) and should satisfy the following demands:  
928	a)  That it have sport-specific exercises and tasks that simulate forthcoming 
929	competitive activity and it develops mental readiness and toughness; 
930	b)  That it develops maximal speed (power) abilities and sport-specific quickness; 
931	c)  That it offers full restoration after highly fatiguing workloads in the preceding 
932	transmutation mesocycle.

discipline (Figure 3.6).  The key factor in creating or using specialized exercises for 
development of special strength or explosive strength in highly coordinated sports 
events is that the coach understand technique of the skill and then couple it with the 
exercise.  In other words, the strength or explosive exercise duplicates (simulates) the 
technique so that both technique and strength are improved simultaneously as used in 
competition (Yessis, 2006).

It is worth noting that the corresponding microcycle in the jump events has 
many specific features like sprint exercises, etc. Nevertheless, the above mentioned 
particulars (Figure 3.6) remain relevant for other explosive strength disciplines. 
  
When considering microcycle design in explosive strength (power) sports, 
special attention should be given to the suppressive impact of excessive fatigue 
accumulation. This detrimental effect appears most particularly in the neural and 
hormonal spheres among athletes. It is well known that explosive strength depends on 

===== PDF PAGE 104 =====

93 
 
sensitivity and reactivity of the neuro-muscular system and that excessive fatigue 
disrupts the subtle regulation of neural input and muscle contraction. The hormonal 
effect also plays a decisive role in training responses to explosive strength sessions.  
Testosterone as the primary male sex hormone, determines the anabolic effect of 
strength training.  In addition, its variations during athletic training indicate the level 
of induced physical stress (Viru and Viru, 2000). For example, the influence of 
testosterone on explosive performance was examined in a special study (Cardinale 
and Stone, 2006) 
 
Case study . Seventy elite athletes in track and field (sprinters), handball, 
volleyball and soccer players (a total of 22 women and 48 men) participated. 
Resting testosterone levels in blood and height of a countermovement vertical 
jump were examined after 10 hours of fasting and one day of rest. A significant 
positive relationship was found between testosterone levels and jump performance 
(r = 0.61, p <0.001). Thus, testosterone levels strongly affect power output in 
muscular efforts having short contraction times (Cardinale and Stone, 2006). 
 
  
The study findings lead to at least two conclusions for explosive strength 
training: 
1)  persons with relatively high testosterone levels (both male and female athletes) 
have an inherited predisposition for explosive strength performance; 
2)  the training design in microcycles for explosive strength development should 
avoid excessive fatigue that suppresses the testosterone level and sharply 
reduces the effect of maximal power exercises.  
  
3.1.6. Pre-competitive microcycle 
 
The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization mesocycle 
(1.2.2) and should satisfy the following demands:  
a)  That it have sport-specific exercises and tasks that simulate forthcoming 
competitive activity and it develops mental readiness and toughness; 
b)  That it develops maximal speed (power) abilities and sport-specific quickness; 
c)  That it offers full restoration after highly fatiguing workloads in the preceding 
transmutation mesocycle. 

===== PDF PAGE 105 =====

94 
 
There is one more demand that relates to mental readiness for forthcoming 
competition.  Its importance increases as the competition approaches, although mental 
preparation is incorporated into the training process at earlier stages as well.  
 
 Because the pre-competitive microcycle is part of the realization mesocycle, 
also called the taper, its methodological clarification and interpretation is quite 
different. Basically, it is intended to reduce the total workloads but the ways of 
attaining this goal vary. It is generally believed that total training volume should be 
decreased but many contradictions exist regarding workout duration and frequency of 
high intensity exercises (Kubukeli et al., 2002). The Block Periodization concept 
makes it possible to propose general approaches that can assist in designing the pre-
competitive microcycle in several sports (Table 3.5).

1003	 Reduction of workload volume is a principal condit ion for full restoration in 
1004	order to attain and then exploit, the state of supercompensation. In other words, 
1005	reduction of the workload level is of primary importance but how it is done is based 
1006	on different circumstances. The main factors in workload decrease are (1) a reduction 
1007	in total training volume and (2) a reduction in partial volume of the intense exercises. 
1008	The proportions are sport-specific and depend on the individual, but the outcome is 
1009	always similar – restoration and improvement of the athlete's general state. This 
1010	improved condition forms the background for the successful employment of two 
1011	groups of exercises: 
1012	- maximal speed drills (recall that their effect depends on the reactivity of the 
1013	central nervous system and the availability of energy resources), and 
1014	- sport-specific tasks simulating forthcoming techno-tactical competitive 
1015	situations (well restored athletes can better approach model competitive 
1016	regimes and adjust better to expected stressors). 
1017	 
1018	Workout frequency, as a component of microcycle design, is neither simple 
1019	nor unequivocal. On the one hand, reduced frequency can be considered as a way to 
1020	decrease total workloads and to find more time for restoration.  On the other hand, the 
1021	division of daily workloads into two sessions makes it possible to increase the quality 
1022	of highly intense exercises.  Additional free time, particularly in the pre-competitive 
1023	training camp, can be a serious disadvantage to the daily program. Thus, the preferred 
1024	solution is to maintain the usual daily schedule for these athletes. In qualified athletes, 
1025	particularly during the pre-competitive training camp, this means performing eight-ten 
1026	workouts per week. 
1027	 
1028	Workout organization in the pre-competitive microcycle is strongly dependent 
1029	on the specificity of the sport and individual characteristics of the athletes. Of course, 
1030	in team sports and team events such as rhythmic gymnastics or events in rowing and 
1031	canoeing, group workouts are dominant. Nevertheless, the general tendency is toward 
1032	a relative increase in individual workouts, where athletes can better concentrate on 
1033	personal technical details, feelings, responses and proper ways of self-regulation. 
1034	Also, proper contact with the coach affects the athletes' self-confidence. 
1035	 
1036	
1037	===== PDF PAGE 107 =====
1038	
1039	96 
1040	 
1041	The restorative workouts contribute more in this training plan than in other 
1042	microcycles. This is explained, first of all, by the importance of the restorative process 
1043	in the entire taper program and in attaining the supercompensation state for the 
1044	competition period. In addition, because the time allocation is more liberal in the pre-
1045	competitive microcycle, there is better exploitation of restorative workouts and the 
1046	use of exercises as tools to increase the quality of the most important sport-specific 
1047	sessions. 
1048	 
1049	Special attention should be given to the proper timing of workouts with regard 
1050	to the expected schedule of competitions. In general, the daily biological rhythms 
1051	should be adjusted to the schedule of the forthcoming competition, i.e., the most 
1052	important workouts should be planned for the time of competitive peak-performance.  
1053	 
1054	Example . The canoe-kayak and rowing regatta programs at the Olympic Games 
1055	from 1984-2004 were scheduled exclusively for the morning hours. This is in 
1056	contrast to the program of world and continental championships in which races are 
1057	held both in the morning and afternoon hours. Consequently, pre-Olympic 
1058	preparation of world-class rowers and paddlers is planned in keeping with the 
1059	expected time of maximal effort. This is especially typical of pre-competitive 
1060	microcycles, where athletes perform sport specific simulative exercises in time for 
1061	the forthcoming events.  
1062	      
1063	 The general chart of the pre-competitive microcycl e presented here was 
1064	compiled for training camp conditions and for expected competitive peak-
1065	performance times in the morning hours (Figure 3.7).

1133	maximal or/and explosive strength allows athletes to maintain the technical force

1135	for muscular hypertrophy prevent the uncontrolled reduction of muscle mass induced

1141	In-season preparation of high-performance team and dual sport athletes 
1142	has very specific demands when applying the BP approach to training design. 
1143	The sports season in soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball, etc. lasts 20-35

1150	very limited. In the typical situation, players maintain their strength abilities near 
1151	pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks; afterwards, strength variables decrease 
1152	dramatically (Fleck and Kraemer, 1997). The normal time span between the 
1153	games (one week) doesn’t allow effective work on the many disparate training 
1154	targets such as metabolic conditioning, maximal and explosive strength, injury 
1155	prevention, techno-tactical skills, game-specific endurance and active restoration. 
1156	Thus, training priorities should be strictly determined and based on them, several 
1157	approaches of BP can be incorporated: 
1158	- high concentration of specialized workloads within mini-blocks; 
1159	- separation of mini-blocks directed at different training modalities; 
1160	- determination of key-workouts.
