1216	dominant training target. The mini-block begins with a workout for active 
1217	recovery using medium or low load levels of aerobic and general conditioning 
1218	exercises. The dominant target should be achieved in two key-workouts, 
1219	which are combined with medium load level team practice (Tuesday 
1220	afternoon) and a conditioning restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon). 
1221	Thus, strength exercises as the important component of key-workouts, are 
1222	followed by 28-30 hours of recovery that facilitates the anabolic process and 
1223	restoration prior to the 2 nd  mini-block.  
1224	 
1225	2)  The 2 nd  mini-block (Thursday- Saturday) targets sport-specific team practice 
1226	and immediate preparation for the forthcoming game. It includes two 
1227	obligatory team-practices. One of them precedes the day off and is intended to 
1228	produce a pronounced game-specific training stimulus. The second workout 
1229	immediately precedes the game, but with a restricted load level. Its content is 
1230	usually connected with the expected particulars of the forthcoming match and 
1231	as such, contains mostly techno-tactical drills.  
1232	 
1233	Several highly motivated players and teams perform the in-season 
1234	training microcycle without a day off. In this case the optional conditioning or 
1235	techno-tactical workout can be executed on Friday morning (this optional 
1236	session is not indicated on the figure). The possible merits of such planning 
1237	are obvious.  They facilitate the perfection of individual and/or collective 
1238	techno-tactical skills and maintain the general conditioning level. The 
1239	negatives of such a microcycle design are obvious as well – usually the 
1240	players demand an entire day for their personal needs and mental recovery. 
1241	 
1242	3)  The microcycle chart presented above gives prio rity to maximal strength 
1243	development whereas explosive-type performances belong to the secondary 
1244	target. Such an emphasis on a maximum strength program is based on the 
1245	need for maintaining a favorable somatic, functional and anabolic status. 
1246	Nevertheless there are examples of sequencing classic high-resistance training

1256	weekly competition, restrict the benefits of utilizing BP mesocycle sequencing. 
1257	However, the benefits of accentuating dominant training targets, in a mini-block 
1258	structure, and designing key-workouts can be attained despite variations in sports and

1307	In addition to the above schematic, a number of general rules can be proposed 
1308	to facilitate microcycle training design.   
1309	 
1310	The first rule – priority of key-workouts. The content and training modality of 
1311	the key-workouts determine the main effect and direction of the whole microcycle.  
1312	Thus, when the targeted abilities of a microcycle are clearly defined, the training 
1313	design should start by structuring the key-workouts. 
1314	 
1315	The second rule – arrangement of key-workouts.  When structuring the 
1316	sessions adjacent to key-workouts, their interaction should be taken into account.  The 
1317	preceding workout affects the athlete's sensitivity to developing workloads while the 
1318	subsequent session determines fatigue accumulation and the restorative process. 
1319	 
1320	The third rule – sharing restorative means. The restorative means, i.e., 
1321	restorative workouts, restorative exercises (low intensity aerobic exercises, stretching, 
1322	relaxation, shaking, breathing exercises), and restorative procedures (massage, sauna, 
1323	hydro- and physiotherapy, mental training) form an indispensable component of 
1324	training design. These means should be expertly planned in the framework of each 
1325	microcycle. 
1326	 
1327	The fourth rule - workload initiation and workload peaks. Usually a day-off 
1328	decreases the athletes readiness for high workloads. Thus, the first session of the 
1329	microcylcle should not be a key-workout. The number and placement of the key-
1330	workouts determine where the peak occurs and how many there are in the microcycle, 
1331	i.e., one-peak, two-peak and three-peak designs. 
1332	 
1333	The fifth rule – monitoring the training. The data from key-workout execution 
1334	provide the best indication of the athletes’ current state.  This includes his current 
1335	achievements, technical variables being performed at the required level, his responses, 
1336	i.e., heart rate, blood lactate concentration, rate of perceived exertion, etc.

1346	3.2. Mesocycles 
1347	 
1348	The Block Periodization concept proposes three types of mesocycles (Table 
1349	1.7). As explained in Chapter 1, their general assessment and interpretation differ 
1350	considerably from traditional training theory. Indeed, mesocycle-blocks form the 
1351	essence of this alternative approach. They encompass both the extensive experience of 
1352	prominent coaches in different sports and new concepts that clarify modern training. 
1353	Thus, accumulation, transmutation and realization mesocycles will be considered in 
1354	light of Block Periodization. 
1355	 
1356	3.2.1. Accumulation mesocycle 
1357	 
1358	 In comparison to other mesocycles, this type is characterized by relatively 
1359	high volumes of workloads at relatively reduced intensity. As the accumulation 
1360	mesocycle is intended to develop basic athletic abilities, its duration, content and 
1361	monitoring are of particular interest. 
1362	 
1363	Duration . In general, two major factors impact the length of this mesocycle:  
1364	- sufficient time to attain the desired cumulative training effect in the targeted 
1365	motor abilities; 
1366	- the time limitation dictated by the competitive calendar. 
1367	 
1368	It has already been noted that the basic motor abilities developed in the 
1369	majority of sports are aerobic endurance and maximal muscle strength. Progress in 
1370	both of these abilities demands profound morphological and even organic changes.  
1371	Therefore, sufficient time is needed for the physiological adaptation to take place. 
1372	However, among qualified athletes having high levels of general fitness, relatively 
1373	short periods of accentuated workloads provide substantial improvement in these 
1374	abilities. Thus, it is important to determine the optimal duration for the mesocycle-
1375	block that will be sufficient to attain the desired changes but not excessively long so 
1376	that the next mesocycle can start on time. This can be illustrated by the outcomes of a 
1377	relevant case study. 
1378	 
1379	 
1380

1385	Case study . Eight highly qualified female kayakers were monitored during a 
1386	twenty week training program aimed at improving maximal strength abilities and 
1387	aerobic endurance. High-resistance training lasted 4-5 hr/week; monitored by the 
1388	measurement of maximal isometric force in kayak-specific body positions. The gain 
1389	in maximal strength and the improvement rate differed greatly at the beginning, 
1390	middle and end of the program (Figure 3.9). The initial three weeks induced average 
1391	strength increases equal to 5.9%, i.e., an improvement rate of 1.93% per week; the 
1392	next three weeks showed additional improvement of 1.6% and an improvement rate of 
1393	0.53%.  Continuation of the program had a very modest impact, where the 
1394	improvement rate decreased to 0.25 and 0.13% per week. Therefore, the entire fitness 
1395	program was very effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six 
1396	weeks and had only a minor effect for the next 14 weeks (based on Sharobajko, 
1397	1984).

1432	motor abilities but also by profound changes in physiological systems. This is 
1433	particularly relevant in early season preparation when enhancement of basic abilities 
1434	and functions is of special importance. Therefore, the accumulation mesocycle can be

1437	stimulate basic abilities and refresh general responses.

1439	The time limits imposed by the competition calendar have a strong impact on 
1440	mesocycle planning. Early in the season, athletes are usually less dependent on 
1441	competition scheduling.  In such cases the mesocycle duration can be based 
1442	exclusively on coaching concepts. At mid-season, the timing of important 
1443	competitions dictates the sequence and duration of training stages.  Consequently, the 
1444	accumulation mesocycle can be shortened to three-four weeks while at the end of the 
1445	season, important competitions can come at relatively short intervals and the length of 
1446	the accumulation mesocycle can be reduced to 10-14 days.

===== PDF PAGE 106 =====

95 
 
 
 Reduction of workload volume is a principal condit ion for full restoration in 
order to attain and then exploit, the state of supercompensation. In other words, 
reduction of the workload level is of primary importance but how it is done is based 
on different circumstances. The main factors in workload decrease are (1) a reduction 
in total training volume and (2) a reduction in partial volume of the intense exercises. 
The proportions are sport-specific and depend on the individual, but the outcome is 
always similar – restoration and improvement of the athlete's general state. This 
improved condition forms the background for the successful employment of two 
groups of exercises: 
- maximal speed drills (recall that their effect depends on the reactivity of the 
central nervous system and the availability of energy resources), and 
- sport-specific tasks simulating forthcoming techno-tactical competitive 
situations (well restored athletes can better approach model competitive 
regimes and adjust better to expected stressors). 
 
Workout frequency, as a component of microcycle design, is neither simple 
nor unequivocal. On the one hand, reduced frequency can be considered as a way to 
decrease total workloads and to find more time for restoration.  On the other hand, the 
division of daily workloads into two sessions makes it possible to increase the quality 
of highly intense exercises.  Additional free time, particularly in the pre-competitive 
training camp, can be a serious disadvantage to the daily program. Thus, the preferred 
solution is to maintain the usual daily schedule for these athletes. In qualified athletes, 
particularly during the pre-competitive training camp, this means performing eight-ten 
workouts per week. 
 
Workout organization in the pre-competitive microcycle is strongly dependent 
on the specificity of the sport and individual characteristics of the athletes. Of course, 
in team sports and team events such as rhythmic gymnastics or events in rowing and 
canoeing, group workouts are dominant. Nevertheless, the general tendency is toward 
a relative increase in individual workouts, where athletes can better concentrate on 
personal technical details, feelings, responses and proper ways of self-regulation. 
Also, proper contact with the coach affects the athletes' self-confidence. 
 

===== PDF PAGE 107 =====

96 
 
The restorative workouts contribute more in this training plan than in other 
microcycles. This is explained, first of all, by the importance of the restorative process 
in the entire taper program and in attaining the supercompensation state for the 
competition period. In addition, because the time allocation is more liberal in the pre-
competitive microcycle, there is better exploitation of restorative workouts and the 
use of exercises as tools to increase the quality of the most important sport-specific 
sessions. 
 
Special attention should be given to the proper timing of workouts with regard 
to the expected schedule of competitions. In general, the daily biological rhythms 
should be adjusted to the schedule of the forthcoming competition, i.e., the most 
important workouts should be planned for the time of competitive peak-performance.  
 
Example . The canoe-kayak and rowing regatta programs at the Olympic Games 
from 1984-2004 were scheduled exclusively for the morning hours. This is in 
contrast to the program of world and continental championships in which races are 
held both in the morning and afternoon hours. Consequently, pre-Olympic 
preparation of world-class rowers and paddlers is planned in keeping with the 
expected time of maximal effort. This is especially typical of pre-competitive 
microcycles, where athletes perform sport specific simulative exercises in time for 
the forthcoming events.  
      
 The general chart of the pre-competitive microcycl e presented here was 
compiled for training camp conditions and for expected competitive peak-
performance times in the morning hours (Figure 3.7).

 It is worth noting the particular role of strength  exercises in the design of pre-
competitive microcycles. On the one hand, many athletes report that high-resistance 
exercises prior to competition negatively affect fine technical skills and the number of 
such exercises should be diminished or even excluded. This stance is especially 
typical among swimmers (Platonov, Fesenko, 1990) but also appears among 
volleyball and tennis players. On the other hand, the use of sport-specific exercises for 
maximal or/and explosive strength allows athletes to maintain the technical force 
component at the desired level (Bompa, Carrera, 2003). In addition, proper exercises 
for muscular hypertrophy prevent the uncontrolled reduction of muscle mass induced 
by stress hormones prior to and during competition.    
 
3.1.7.  Microcycle for sport-specific fitness maintenance in dual and team 
sports .  
 
In-season preparation of high-performance team and dual sport athletes 
has very specific demands when applying the BP approach to training design. 
The sports season in soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball, etc. lasts 20-35 

===== PDF PAGE 109 =====

98 
 
weeks where the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is 
very limited. In the typical situation, players maintain their strength abilities near 
pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks; afterwards, strength variables decrease 
dramatically (Fleck and Kraemer, 1997). The normal time span between the 
games (one week) doesn’t allow effective work on the many disparate training 
targets such as metabolic conditioning, maximal and explosive strength, injury 
prevention, techno-tactical skills, game-specific endurance and active restoration. 
Thus, training priorities should be strictly determined and based on them, several 
approaches of BP can be incorporated: 
- high concentration of specialized workloads within mini-blocks; 
- separation of mini-blocks directed at different training modalities; 
- determination of key-workouts. 
The diagram in Figure 3.8 presents the proposed microcycle design.

===== PDF PAGE 110 =====

99 
 
In the microcycle chart in Figure 3.8, the following particulars are worth noting: 
 
1)  The 1 st  mini-block (Monday- Wednesday) is devoted to mainly development 
of sport-specific strength abilities, i.e., maximal and explosive strength as the 
dominant training target. The mini-block begins with a workout for active 
recovery using medium or low load levels of aerobic and general conditioning 
exercises. The dominant target should be achieved in two key-workouts, 
which are combined with medium load level team practice (Tuesday 
afternoon) and a conditioning restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon). 
Thus, strength exercises as the important component of key-workouts, are 
followed by 28-30 hours of recovery that facilitates the anabolic process and 
restoration prior to the 2 nd  mini-block.  
 
2)  The 2 nd  mini-block (Thursday- Saturday) targets sport-specific team practice 
and immediate preparation for the forthcoming game. It includes two 
obligatory team-practices. One of them precedes the day off and is intended to 
produce a pronounced game-specific training stimulus. The second workout 
immediately precedes the game, but with a restricted load level. Its content is 
usually connected with the expected particulars of the forthcoming match and 
as such, contains mostly techno-tactical drills.  
 
Several highly motivated players and teams perform the in-season 
training microcycle without a day off. In this case the optional conditioning or 
techno-tactical workout can be executed on Friday morning (this optional 
session is not indicated on the figure). The possible merits of such planning 
are obvious.  They facilitate the perfection of individual and/or collective 
techno-tactical skills and maintain the general conditioning level. The 
negatives of such a microcycle design are obvious as well – usually the 
players demand an entire day for their personal needs and mental recovery. 
 
3)  The microcycle chart presented above gives prio rity to maximal strength 
development whereas explosive-type performances belong to the secondary 
target. Such an emphasis on a maximum strength program is based on the 
need for maintaining a favorable somatic, functional and anabolic status. 
Nevertheless there are examples of sequencing classic high-resistance training 

===== PDF PAGE 111 =====

100 
 
with microcycles of ballistic explosive-type exercises that help to enhance 
jump performance (Newton et al., 2006).   
 
The short time span and the emotional and physical stress associated with 
weekly competition, restrict the benefits of utilizing BP mesocycle sequencing. 
However, the benefits of accentuating dominant training targets, in a mini-block 
structure, and designing key-workouts can be attained despite variations in sports and 
local conditions. 
 
 3.1.8. How to construct a microcycle   
 
The Block Periodization approach entails several specific considerations concerning 
microcycle construction. They relate to the function and importance of key-workouts.  
This includes: determination and compilation of key-workouts, facilitation of 
workload performance in key-workouts, monitoring the training etc. The restorative 
process also takes on greater importance because of the preparation involved in highly 
concentrated workloads and restoration after their execution. In general, the entire 
process of microcycle construction can be presented in a sequence of specific 
operations (Table 3.6).

===== PDF PAGE 112 =====

101 
 
 
In addition to the above schematic, a number of general rules can be proposed 
to facilitate microcycle training design.   
 
The first rule – priority of key-workouts. The content and training modality of 
the key-workouts determine the main effect and direction of the whole microcycle.  
Thus, when the targeted abilities of a microcycle are clearly defined, the training 
design should start by structuring the key-workouts. 
 
The second rule – arrangement of key-workouts.  When structuring the 
sessions adjacent to key-workouts, their interaction should be taken into account.  The 
preceding workout affects the athlete's sensitivity to developing workloads while the 
subsequent session determines fatigue accumulation and the restorative process. 
 
The third rule – sharing restorative means. The restorative means, i.e., 
restorative workouts, restorative exercises (low intensity aerobic exercises, stretching, 
relaxation, shaking, breathing exercises), and restorative procedures (massage, sauna, 
hydro- and physiotherapy, mental training) form an indispensable component of 
training design. These means should be expertly planned in the framework of each 
microcycle. 
 
The fourth rule - workload initiation and workload peaks. Usually a day-off 
decreases the athletes readiness for high workloads. Thus, the first session of the 
microcylcle should not be a key-workout. The number and placement of the key-
workouts determine where the peak occurs and how many there are in the microcycle, 
i.e., one-peak, two-peak and three-peak designs. 
 
The fifth rule – monitoring the training. The data from key-workout execution 
provide the best indication of the athletes’ current state.  This includes his current 
achievements, technical variables being performed at the required level, his responses, 
i.e., heart rate, blood lactate concentration, rate of perceived exertion, etc.  
 
 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 113 =====

102 
 
3.2. Mesocycles 
 
The Block Periodization concept proposes three types of mesocycles (Table 
1.7). As explained in Chapter 1, their general assessment and interpretation differ 
considerably from traditional training theory. Indeed, mesocycle-blocks form the 
essence of this alternative approach. They encompass both the extensive experience of 
prominent coaches in different sports and new concepts that clarify modern training. 
Thus, accumulation, transmutation and realization mesocycles will be considered in 
light of Block Periodization. 
 
3.2.1. Accumulation mesocycle 
 
 In comparison to other mesocycles, this type is characterized by relatively 
high volumes of workloads at relatively reduced intensity. As the accumulation 
mesocycle is intended to develop basic athletic abilities, its duration, content and 
monitoring are of particular interest. 
 
Duration . In general, two major factors impact the length of this mesocycle:  
- sufficient time to attain the desired cumulative training effect in the targeted 
motor abilities; 
- the time limitation dictated by the competitive calendar. 
 
It has already been noted that the basic motor abilities developed in the 
majority of sports are aerobic endurance and maximal muscle strength. Progress in 
both of these abilities demands profound morphological and even organic changes.  
Therefore, sufficient time is needed for the physiological adaptation to take place. 
However, among qualified athletes having high levels of general fitness, relatively 
short periods of accentuated workloads provide substantial improvement in these 
abilities. Thus, it is important to determine the optimal duration for the mesocycle-
block that will be sufficient to attain the desired changes but not excessively long so 
that the next mesocycle can start on time. This can be illustrated by the outcomes of a 
relevant case study. 
 
 

===== PDF PAGE 114 =====

103 
 
Case study . Eight highly qualified female kayakers were monitored during a 
twenty week training program aimed at improving maximal strength abilities and 
aerobic endurance. High-resistance training lasted 4-5 hr/week; monitored by the 
measurement of maximal isometric force in kayak-specific body positions. The gain 
in maximal strength and the improvement rate differed greatly at the beginning, 
middle and end of the program (Figure 3.9). The initial three weeks induced average 
strength increases equal to 5.9%, i.e., an improvement rate of 1.93% per week; the 
next three weeks showed additional improvement of 1.6% and an improvement rate of 
0.53%.  Continuation of the program had a very modest impact, where the 
improvement rate decreased to 0.25 and 0.13% per week. Therefore, the entire fitness 
program was very effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six 
weeks and had only a minor effect for the next 14 weeks (based on Sharobajko, 
1984).

 Similar trends have been noted during prolonged pr ograms to improve aerobic 
endurance.  This corresponds to the general biological concept that the adaptive 
response induced by long-term training declines with time (Bouchard, 1986). All of 
the above further supports the general idea underlying Block Periodization--that 
training should be divided into shorter periods and use higher improvement rates for 
developing different abilities. 
 
The cumulative training effect is characterized not only by gains in specific 
motor abilities but also by profound changes in physiological systems. This is 
particularly relevant in early season preparation when enhancement of basic abilities 
and functions is of special importance. Therefore, the accumulation mesocycle can be 
longer (up to six weeks) when training is intended to elicit more profound 
physiological changes, or shorter (three weeks or less) when training is intended to 
stimulate basic abilities and refresh general responses.  
  
The time limits imposed by the competition calendar have a strong impact on 
mesocycle planning. Early in the season, athletes are usually less dependent on 
competition scheduling.  In such cases the mesocycle duration can be based 
exclusively on coaching concepts. At mid-season, the timing of important 
competitions dictates the sequence and duration of training stages.  Consequently, the 
accumulation mesocycle can be shortened to three-four weeks while at the end of the 
season, important competitions can come at relatively short intervals and the length of 
the accumulation mesocycle can be reduced to 10-14 days.   
  
Content.  The selection and sequence of appropriate microcycles substantially 
determine mesocycle content in terms of load variation (Table 3.7).

2029	Nutrition during the realization mesocycle should be given special attention 
2030	especially in regard to balancing dietary intake and energy expenditure. As was 
2031	emphasized, workload reduction is characteristic of this mesocycle. Correspondingly, 
2032	energy expenditure decreases significantly while athletes' nutritional habits often 
2033	remain unchanged. As a result, energy intake can surpass energy expenditure causing 
2034	a noticeable increase in the fat component.  
2035	 
2036	 
2037	Case study . Twenty highly qualified male long-distance triathletes were 
2038	monitored during a four-week mesocycle with high workloads and a subsequent 
2039	two-week taper mesocycle with reduced workloads. Body mass, body fat, energy 
2040	intake and expenditure were evaluated. It was found that the average energy 
2041	intake remained at the same level, but energy expenditure decreased during the 
2042	taper mesocycle by up to 69.3% (Figure 3.10).  Mean body mass of the group 
2043	didn’t change but body fat mass increased by 4.3%. The imbalance of dietary 
2044	intake and energy expenditure caused remarkable fat accumulation. However, it is 
2045	also possible that their muscle mass decreased as well while body mass remained 
2046	at the previous level. Therefore, body mass as an indicator of the anthropometric 
2047	state, is not always reliable.  The pre-competition reduction of training workloads 
2048	requires attention to nutrition, which should correspond to the decreased energy 
2049	expenditure (based on Margaritis et al., 2003).

2079	3.3. Training stage 
2080	 
2081	According to Block Periodization, three consecutive mesocycle-blocks form a 
2082	single training stage. Its length depends on the duration of each mesocycle and varies 
2083	from 4-10 weeks.  As was already noted (1.2.3), the training stage reconstructs the 
2084	entire annual cycle in miniature.  This allows for the consecutive development of 
2085	basic abilities (as in the preparatory period), specific abilities (as in the competitive 
2086	period), and integrative readiness for event-specific performance. The most favorable 
2087	carry-over of residual training effects makes it possible to attain the optimal 
2088	combination of basic, special and event-specific abilities as needed at the moment of 
2089	competition (Figure 1.8). However, if the training design is based solely on the length 
2090	of training residuals, it will be extremely rigid and inflexible. There are also other 
2091	factors influencing training residuals and additional methods to prolong them.

2098	3.3.1. Competition in the training stage .   
2099	 
2100	 It is well known that not all competitions are pla nned for peak performance. 
2101	Some of them include extraordinarily high workloads to break the training routine and 
2102	to add emotional diversity to the preparation. With this aim in mind, competition can 
2103	be included in the accumulation and transmutation mesocycles. However, their 
2104	influence is unequivocal. Highly intense competitions produce profound physical and 
2105	emotional stress. The secretion of stress hormones like catecholamines and cortisol, 
2106	modulate the athletes’ metabolic response and reinforce the catabolic process (Viru & 
2107	Viru, 2001). As a result, muscle mass and maximum strength can decrease.  
2108	 
2109	Moreover, the highly intense anaerobic glycolitic efforts typical in competition 
2110	suppress the activity of aerobic enzymes and the oxidative process in the 
2111	mitochondria (Volkov, 1986).  This impairment of aerobic fitness has been noted for 
2112	some time by prominent coaches rather intuitively.  They added special aerobic 
2113	workloads to restore and revitalize the athletes after competition. A recent publication 
2114	elucidates this negative effect of competition because of the shortened training 
2115	residuals (Issurin & Lustig, 2004).  
2116	  
2117	Case study .  The preparation of multi- Olympic and World swimming 
2118	champion Alexandre Popov was monitored using an incremental stepwise 
2119	swimming test. His anaerobic threshold speed was determined at a blood lactate 
2120	level of 4 mM and a speed producing 8 mM, as the lower limit of highly intense 
2121	glycolitic workloads. These indicators were evaluated at the beginning of the 
2122	mesocycle with highly concentrated aerobic workloads, ten days after this 
2123	evaluation, and a few days after the competition in which Alexandre performed 
2124	several times (Figure 3.11). In the initial stage of this study the remarkable gain 
2125	in both anaerobic threshold speed and speed corresponding to 8 mM  was noted. 
2126	However, upon measurement of these factors again after competition, a 
2127	substantial decrease was seen.  This can be attributed to shortened training 
2128	residuals, induced by the previous program (adapted from Pyne & 
2129	Touretski,1993).

2172	residual training effects after the first accumulation mesocycle which lasts about 30 
2173	days (Table 1.6). This timing determines the total duration of the second and third 
2174	mesocycles, which should not be longer than the training residuals of the aerobic and 
2175	strength workloads, i.e., one month. However, in many sports the transmutation

2183	about two weeks. The duration of both of these mesocycles (about five weeks) 
2184	exceeds the time of the strength-aerobic training residuals that may cause the athletes 
2185	to approach the targeted competition at a reduced level of basic abilities.

2188	training residuals of the strength-aerobic program. This prolongation can be attained

2191	strongly suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training and the anabolic strength 
2192	exercises require sufficient recovery that cannot be provided. Apparently, what should 
2193	be inserted in the mesocycle is not several additional workouts but a special compact 
2194	mini-block (short microcycle), in order to prolong training residuals. This principal 
2195	approach is displayed in Figure 3.12.

2234	residuals following the accumulation mesocycle surpass the competition.

2237	sports where the international calendar has no competitions scheduled before the

2243	Microcycles, as the shortest training cycles, are differentiated in three 
2244	principle ways, loading, competing and recovery. The microcycles devoted to loading 
2245	differ according to load level. There is adjustment  that serves to adapt athletes to 
2246	increasing workloads, loading  that is used to develop athletic abilities, and impact  that 
2247	employs extreme training stimuli. The competing microcycle contains the pre-
2248	competitive  microcycle, which prepares the athlete for forthcoming competitions and 
2249	the competitive  microcycle, where the athlete takes part in the competition. The 
2250	recovery microcycle consists of a special restoration  microcycle. The microcycles can 
2251	be managed with respect to different load variations. More specifically, one-, two-, 
2252	and three-peak designs can be executed.

2254	Presented in this chapter are microcycles focusing on (a) aerobic (strength-
2255	aerobic) abilities, (b) highly intense anaerobic workloads, (c) explosive strength in 
2256	highly coordinated exercises, and (d) pre-competitive training. These microcycles 
2257	have guidelines for structuring the microcycle. A number of general rules for 
2258	constructing the microcycle are as follows: (1) priority of the most meaningful key-
2259	workouts (2) interaction of successive workouts (3) sharing of restoration means (4) 
2260	initiating and peaking training workloads, and (5) monitoring the training.

2268	are considered with respect to duration, content and monitoring of training.

2270	described with respect to the sequencing of various microcycles.  Also covered is 
2271	fatigue accumulation that is particularly pronounced in the transmutation mesocycle, 
2272	the selection of appropriate tasks and exercises, and determination of the most 
2273	adequate means of monitoring several mesocycles. It is important to remember that 
2274	athletes’ self-estimation of training response in their log-book can provide valuable 
2275	information for preventing excessive fatigue and even overtraining. Subjective ratings 
2276	of stress, fatigue, quality of sleep and muscle soreness on a scale of 1 (very, very low 
2277	or good) to 7 (very, very high or bad) are recommended for systematic use.

2280	annual cycle in miniature, where training stimuli are focused first on basic abilities, 
2281	second on more specific abilities, and third on integrative readiness for event-specific 
2282	performance. It is essential to remember that competitive performances and emotional 
2283	strain can shorten the training residuals of the preceding mesocycle.  This 
2284	phenomenon was considered through a case-study example of multi- Olympic 
2285	champion Alexander Popov, whose anaerobic threshold speed decreased significantly 
2286	after competition. Inclusion of special compact mini-blocks (short microcycles) can 
2287	prolong the residual training effects of the preceding mesocycle. Thus, aerobic mini-
2288	blocks can be inserted in the transmutation mesocycle and a highly intense anaerobic 
2289	mini-block can be incorporated within the realization mesocycle.

glycolitic workloads. These indicators were evaluated at the beginning of the 
mesocycle with highly concentrated aerobic workloads, ten days after this 
evaluation, and a few days after the competition in which Alexandre performed 
several times (Figure 3.11). In the initial stage of this study the remarkable gain 
in both anaerobic threshold speed and speed corresponding to 8 mM  was noted. 
However, upon measurement of these factors again after competition, a 
substantial decrease was seen.  This can be attributed to shortened training 
residuals, induced by the previous program (adapted from Pyne & 
Touretski,1993).

 To conclude this section, the following relevant f actors are worth noting: 
1)  Incorporating mid- and low-level competitions in the training stage is an 
important and meaningful component of the entire preparation; 
2)  Competitive performances elicit superior and profound athletes’ responses that 
enrich the spectrum of adaptation to the training routine.  However; 
3)  Highly intense competitive efforts bring about secretion of stress hormones 
that modulate metabolic and hormonal responses and shorten the residual 
training effects of the preceding mesocycle. This should be taken into account 
in the subsequent program.  
 
3.3.2.  How to prolong the residual training effects 
 
 Inasmuch as the training stage is a sequence of th ree mesocycle-blocks, the 
crucial factor that restricts the length of a particular stage is the duration of the 
residual training effects after the first accumulation mesocycle which lasts about 30 
days (Table 1.6). This timing determines the total duration of the second and third 
mesocycles, which should not be longer than the training residuals of the aerobic and 
strength workloads, i.e., one month. However, in many sports the transmutation 

===== PDF PAGE 130 =====

119 
 
mesocycle is directed at reinforcing anaerobic glycolitic abilities, which takes three-
four weeks.  In addition, the duration of the realization mesocycle (taper) can last 
about two weeks. The duration of both of these mesocycles (about five weeks) 
exceeds the time of the strength-aerobic training residuals that may cause the athletes 
to approach the targeted competition at a reduced level of basic abilities.  
 
It is obvious that some special measures should be undertaken to prolong the 
training residuals of the strength-aerobic program. This prolongation can be attained 
by additional supporting workouts for aerobic endurance and/or muscular strength. 
But, such additions are not successful. The highly intense transmutation mesocycle 
strongly suppresses the immediate effect of aerobic training and the anabolic strength 
exercises require sufficient recovery that cannot be provided. Apparently, what should 
be inserted in the mesocycle is not several additional workouts but a special compact 
mini-block (short microcycle), in order to prolong training residuals. This principal 
approach is displayed in Figure 3.12.

Example . Imagine a situation in which two targeted competitions have a 
five-week interval between them (this situation is very typical for kayaking 
where the European and World championships are separated by an interval of 
five-six weeks). In this case of inflexible time limits, you can plan 10-14 days for 
accumulation, 10-14 days for transmutation, and 8-10 days for the realization 
mesocycles. Here you need not include mini-blocks because the training 
residuals following the accumulation mesocycle surpass the competition. 
Another situation occurs when you are forced to plan a training stage for a period 
of 7-9 weeks (this situation is very typical of pre-Olympic preparation in several 
sports where the international calendar has no competitions scheduled before the 
major event). In this case, it is reasonable to plan longer mesocycles and the 
inclusion of mini-blocks would be necessary.    
  
 
Summary 
Microcycles, as the shortest training cycles, are differentiated in three 
principle ways, loading, competing and recovery. The microcycles devoted to loading 
differ according to load level. There is adjustment  that serves to adapt athletes to 
increasing workloads, loading  that is used to develop athletic abilities, and impact  that 
employs extreme training stimuli. The competing microcycle contains the pre-
competitive  microcycle, which prepares the athlete for forthcoming competitions and 
the competitive  microcycle, where the athlete takes part in the competition. The 
recovery microcycle consists of a special restoration  microcycle. The microcycles can 
be managed with respect to different load variations. More specifically, one-, two-, 
and three-peak designs can be executed.  
 
Presented in this chapter are microcycles focusing on (a) aerobic (strength-
aerobic) abilities, (b) highly intense anaerobic workloads, (c) explosive strength in 
highly coordinated exercises, and (d) pre-competitive training. These microcycles 
have guidelines for structuring the microcycle. A number of general rules for 
constructing the microcycle are as follows: (1) priority of the most meaningful key-
workouts (2) interaction of successive workouts (3) sharing of restoration means (4) 
initiating and peaking training workloads, and (5) monitoring the training.  
  

===== PDF PAGE 132 =====

121 
 
The three types of mesocycles proposed by the Block Periodization Concept 
are considered with respect to duration, content and monitoring of training. 
Specifically, the accumulation, transmutation and  realization  mesocycles are 
described with respect to the sequencing of various microcycles.  Also covered is 
fatigue accumulation that is particularly pronounced in the transmutation mesocycle, 
the selection of appropriate tasks and exercises, and determination of the most 
adequate means of monitoring several mesocycles. It is important to remember that 
athletes’ self-estimation of training response in their log-book can provide valuable 
information for preventing excessive fatigue and even overtraining. Subjective ratings 
of stress, fatigue, quality of sleep and muscle soreness on a scale of 1 (very, very low 
or good) to 7 (very, very high or bad) are recommended for systematic use.  
  
The training stage, consisting of three sequenced mesocycles, reconstructs the 
annual cycle in miniature, where training stimuli are focused first on basic abilities, 
second on more specific abilities, and third on integrative readiness for event-specific 
performance. It is essential to remember that competitive performances and emotional 
strain can shorten the training residuals of the preceding mesocycle.  This 
phenomenon was considered through a case-study example of multi- Olympic 
champion Alexander Popov, whose anaerobic threshold speed decreased significantly 
after competition. Inclusion of special compact mini-blocks (short microcycles) can 
prolong the residual training effects of the preceding mesocycle. Thus, aerobic mini-
blocks can be inserted in the transmutation mesocycle and a highly intense anaerobic 
mini-block can be incorporated within the realization mesocycle.

# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
**5-7 days** — see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 89, printed p. 78) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). The peak/trough pattern itself follows the same
general logic as [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]: concentrating the
week's hardest sessions into one, two, or three peaks (rather than spreading maximal effort
evenly across every day) lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be
performed at a high standard.

**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
short duration, 4-7 days — matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this
section (that comes later, 3.1.7); the load-wave figures here are drawn from individual/dual
sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
of the specific cut-points).

**Example** — A four-week fall-camp block could be read as adjustment (days 1-5, single
practices, medium load) into loading (days 6-14, one-a-days plus early two-a-days) into an
impact microcycle (the hardest stretch of two-a-days, 4-7 days) into a pre-competitive
microcycle in the week before the opener — each transition marked by a deliberate change in
purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.

**Related** — [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (the 5-point scale
this section's point-quantification is built on), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# The Anaerobic Glycolytic Microcycle Trades Restoration for Fatigue-Tolerant, Lactate-Driven Development

**What it is** — Issurin describes the microcycle that forms the content of the transmutation
mesocycle (PDF pp. 97-100, printed pp. 86-89, Table 3.3 and Figure 3.5). Its compatible
modalities (Table 3.3): **strength endurance** (mostly anaerobic; high-resistance drills
inside regular workouts or separate sessions; produces a dual strength-endurance and
anaerobic-metabolism effect), **anaerobic alactic/maximal speed** (used by moderately fatigued
athletes since a well-restored state is usually unavailable here; sprints add diversity and
short-duration power contribution), **low-intensity aerobic exercise** (used throughout as
active restoration, alongside stretching/relaxation), and **movement technique/tactics** (given
prime placement and treated as essential despite metabolic fatigue, because competition itself
imposes comparable fatigue on technique). Issurin gives specific lactate-based intensity
zones: workloads producing **5-8 mM** blood lactate improve maximal aerobic power and
aerobic-anaerobic interaction and are more typical early-to-mid-season; workloads above
**8 mM** target anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity specifically and dominate in the final
weeks before the target competition (PDF pp. 97-98, printed pp. 86-87). The worked ten-workout
chart (Figure 3.5, PDF p. 100, printed p. 89) uses a three-peak load design with six
development workouts (three of them key-workouts) targeting anaerobic glycolytic power,
anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength endurance, buffered by a mid-week restoration
"window" (Wednesday evening) and two medium-load alactic-maintenance sessions.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the defining feature of this microcycle is fatigue
accumulation with insufficient restoration by design (PDF p. 99, printed p. 88): high-load
glycolytic work drives maximal heart rate/cardiac output, maximal oxygen deficit/debt and
blood lactate accumulation, plus a rise in catecholamines and cortisol with testosterone
suppressed for 24+ hours (citing Viru, 1995). At a workout frequency of 6-12 sessions/week,
fatigue accumulation across the microcycle is "inevitable" — the design goal is to manage that
fatigue (through workout sequencing, deliberately-placed restoration, and monitoring) rather
than to avoid it, which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one.

**When to apply** — Structuring the highest-intensity block of a transmutation mesocycle
(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) when the
targeted abilities are anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity and anaerobic-component strength
endurance. Issurin's four stated guidelines for managing the built-in fatigue (PDF p. 99,
printed p. 88): sequence development workouts with expected fatigue accumulation in mind;
treat restoration workouts as a planned, non-optional part of the week; use active
restoration means (stretching, low-intensity drills, massage, physiotherapy, nutritional
support); and prioritize training-response monitoring here specifically. **Inference:** this
maps to the hardest week(s) of fall camp or a mid-season "gut check" conditioning emphasis,
where the department accepts several days of accumulating fatigue in exchange for a
concentrated glycolytic-capacity stimulus, rather than trying to keep every day fresh.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific lactate cut-points (5-8 mM vs. >8 mM) and
the 6-12 workouts/week frequency figure are presented without a cited validation study in this
passage; treat them as Issurin's own applied heuristics. **Inference:** none of this section's
evidence is football-specific — it is framed around individual/dual sports and combat sports
with a season structure that tolerates a dedicated multi-day high-fatigue block, which is
harder to fit inside a single football in-season week (see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the team-sport-adapted version).
**Eric's baseline** explicitly treats glycolytic conditioning for football as something to
absorb incidentally through camp and practice rather than as a primary programmed target
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39)
— a different posture than this microcycle's deliberate, concentrated glycolytic emphasis,
which is drawn from individual/dual/combat-sport programming. Blood lactate testing
capability (needed to hit the stated mM zones precisely) is not a standard part of the
department's documented testing stack per this baseline corpus.

**Example** — A transmutation-mesocycle week built for a combat-sport or team-sport athlete
needing anaerobic capacity could place two key-workouts (Monday and Thursday, per Figure 3.5's
pattern) targeting >8 mM glycolytic capacity work, a Tuesday alactic-maintenance session, a
Wednesday evening restoration window, and Friday/Saturday sessions blending anaerobic
glycolytic power with strength endurance — accepting that athletes will not be fully
restored entering most of these sessions.

**Related** — [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength endurance, buffered by a mid-week restoration
"window" (Wednesday evening) and two medium-load alactic-maintenance sessions.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the defining feature of this microcycle is fatigue
accumulation with insufficient restoration by design (PDF p. 99, printed p. 88): high-load
glycolytic work drives maximal heart rate/cardiac output, maximal oxygen deficit/debt and
blood lactate accumulation, plus a rise in catecholamines and cortisol with testosterone
suppressed for 24+ hours (citing Viru, 1995). At a workout frequency of 6-12 sessions/week,
fatigue accumulation across the microcycle is "inevitable" — the design goal is to manage that
fatigue (through workout sequencing, deliberately-placed restoration, and monitoring) rather
than to avoid it, which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one.

**When to apply** — Structuring the highest-intensity block of a transmutation mesocycle
(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) when the
targeted abilities are anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity and anaerobic-component strength
endurance. Issurin's four stated guidelines for managing the built-in fatigue (PDF p. 99,
printed p. 88): sequence development workouts with expected fatigue accumulation in mind;
treat restoration workouts as a planned, non-optional part of the week; use active
restoration means (stretching, low-intensity drills, massage, physiotherapy, nutritional
support); and prioritize training-response monitoring here specifically. **Inference:** this
maps to the hardest week(s) of fall camp or a mid-season "gut check" conditioning emphasis,
where the department accepts several days of accumulating fatigue in exchange for a
concentrated glycolytic-capacity stimulus, rather than trying to keep every day fresh.

evidence is football-specific — it is framed around individual/dual sports and combat sports
with a season structure that tolerates a dedicated multi-day high-fatigue block, which is
harder to fit inside a single football in-season week (see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the team-sport-adapted version).
**Eric's baseline** explicitly treats glycolytic conditioning for football as something to
absorb incidentally through camp and practice rather than as a primary programmed target
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39)
— a different posture than this microcycle's deliberate, concentrated glycolytic emphasis,
which is drawn from individual/dual/combat-sport programming. Blood lactate testing
capability (needed to hit the stated mM zones precisely) is not a standard part of the
department's documented testing stack per this baseline corpus.

**Example** — A transmutation-mesocycle week built for a combat-sport or team-sport athlete
needing anaerobic capacity could place two key-workouts (Monday and Thursday, per Figure 3.5's
pattern) targeting >8 mM glycolytic capacity work, a Tuesday alactic-maintenance session, a
Wednesday evening restoration window, and Friday/Saturday sessions blending anaerobic
glycolytic power with strength endurance — accepting that athletes will not be fully
restored entering most of these sessions.

# Sedykh's Hammer-Throw Microcycle Puts Explosive Strength Only in Morning, Fresh-Athlete Sessions

**What it is** — Issurin presents the eleven-workout microcycle of two-time Olympic champion
hammer thrower Yuri Sedykh (USSR), as reported by his coach (Bondarchuk, 1986) (PDF pp.
101-103, printed pp. 90-92, Table 3.4 and Figure 3.6). Four essential features: (a)
event-specific explosive-strength exercises (throwing different-weight hammers), the
top-priority target, appear **exclusively** in morning sessions and always in the **initial**
part of the workout, to use the athlete's most favorable physical state for the key-exercise;
(b) maximum-strength exercises (barbell snatch, half squats, good mornings), a supporting
role, are placed in five sessions — four separate evening sessions plus once in the second
part of a morning session; (c) additional explosive-strength work (standing jumps) appears
three times, but never when the athlete is in his best condition, i.e., placed after the
primary explosive work is already done; (d) restorative activity (basketball, swimming,
stretching) is built into the program, including on the day off. Issurin separately cites a
related mechanism study: Cardinale and Stone (2006) measured resting blood testosterone and
countermovement vertical jump in 70 elite athletes (48 men, 22 women; sprinters, handball,
volleyball, soccer) after a 10-hour fast and a rest day, finding a significant positive
relationship between testosterone and jump height (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) (PDF p. 103, printed
p. 92). Issurin's own stated implications from that study: athletes with relatively high
testosterone (either sex) have some inherited predisposition for explosive-strength
performance, and microcycle design for explosive-strength development should avoid excessive
fatigue, because fatigue suppresses testosterone and sharply reduces the training effect of
maximal-power exercises.

**Why it works** — Issurin's stated mechanism (PDF pp. 92-93, printed pp. 92-93 [sic, both
appear on the same printed page 92]) is that explosive strength depends on the sensitivity
and reactivity of the neuromuscular system, and excessive fatigue "disrupts the subtle
regulation of neural input and muscle contraction"; testosterone is named as the hormone
determining strength training's anabolic effect and as an index of induced physical stress
(Viru and Viru, 2000). **Inference:** the placement rule (explosive work only when fresh,
morning, first in the session) follows directly from this same logic already generalized in
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]] — CNS-dependent, high-precision qualities
need a well-rested athlete — this case study is simply that general rule applied to one
specific, historically documented program.

**When to apply** — As a concrete illustration of sequencing explosive/technical power work
at the very start of a session, before any fatigue-inducing supporting work, for athletes
whose primary target ability is explosive strength in a highly coordinated skill.
**Inference:** in football, this maps most directly to skill-position or specialist
explosive-power development (e.g., jump-training or Olympic-lift-variant work meant to
transfer to explosive movement) — placing that work first in a session, before conditioning
or high-volume accessory work, mirrors Sedykh's morning-first placement of hammer throws.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite thrower's program from a single
coach's secondhand report (Bondarchuk, 1986), with no comparison athlete or outcome data
beyond the general BPC narrative already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] — it illustrates a design principle,
not a validated dose-response result. **Inference:** hammer throw is an acyclic, single-effort,
highly technical power event with no contact and no in-competition fatigue accumulation across
a "game," unlike football; the specific workout counts, throw counts, and session splits in
Table 3.4 should not be copied as a template. The testosterone-jump correlation (Cardinale and
Stone, 2006) is cross-sectional and observational (r = 0.61 explains well under half the
variance in jump height) — it identifies an association at one time point in rested athletes,
not a training intervention; it does not establish that raising testosterone directly causes
higher jump performance, only that they covary. Population also spans track, handball,
volleyball and soccer athletes of both sexes, not football specifically.

**Example** — A football skill player's Tuesday lift built around explosive-power development
(e.g., trap-bar jumps, medicine-ball throws) should be sequenced first in the session, on a day
following adequate rest, with any high-volume or fatiguing accessory work placed afterward —
not the reverse.

**Related** — [[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]],
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# The Pre-Competitive Microcycle: Cut Volume Hard, Raise Maximal-Speed and Sport-Specific Work, Keep Frequency

**What it is** — The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization
mesocycle (see [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]) and is also called the
taper at the microcycle level (PDF pp. 104-105, printed pp. 93-94; verified against page
images). It must satisfy three demands (PDF p. 104, printed p. 93): sport-specific
exercises/tasks that simulate the forthcoming competition and build mental readiness and
toughness; development of maximal speed/power and sport-specific quickness; and full (or
partial) restoration after the preceding transmutation mesocycle's fatiguing workloads. Table
3.5 (PDF p. 105, printed p. 94, verified against page image) gives seven prescriptive
characteristics: **workload volume** — substantially reduced, to create conditions for full
recovery; **volume of intense exercises specifically** — substantially reduced versus the
prior mesocycle, so total drill volume falls but quality rises; **contribution of maximum
speed/power exercises** — substantially **increased** (well-rested athletes respond better to
maximal-speed drills, and maximal-speed training residuals are the shortest of any ability, per
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]); **contribution of
sport-specific tasks** — substantially increased (simulative tasks improve adaptation to
expected competitive stressors); **workout frequency** — usually kept **similar** to the
previous mesocycle (subdividing the same total work into more, smaller portions raises
quality per session even as volume falls); **organization** — a rational mix of group,
individual and mixed workouts, weighted somewhat more toward individual work than usual, so
athletes can attend to personal technical detail and coach rapport; **restoration** —
deliberately favorable conditions and an increased volume of restorative exercises/workouts,
since athletes have more free time and motivation to use it. Issurin states that in qualified
athletes, especially during a pre-competitive training camp, maintaining frequency in practice
means **eight to ten workouts per week** even as volume per workout drops (PDF p. 105, printed
p. 94). Workout timing should match the expected competition's daily biological-rhythm window
(example given: Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing regattas run only in the morning, so pre-Olympic
training is scheduled to place peak-effort sessions at that same morning time, PDF p. 106,
printed p. 95). Figure 3.7 (PDF p. 107, printed p. 96) gives a worked chart for a
morning-peak-performance pre-competitive microcycle, alternating maximum-strength/technique
mornings with sport-specific-simulation/alactic afternoons, moving toward heavier
sport-specific-simulation and explosive-strength content later in the week. On strength work
specifically, Issurin notes a real disagreement in the field: many athletes (particularly
swimmers, per Platonov & Fesenko, 1990, and also reported among volleyball and tennis players)
report high-resistance work pre-competition degrades fine technical skill, arguing for
reducing or excluding it; but sport-specific maximal/explosive strength work is also argued to
maintain the technical force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and to prevent uncontrolled,
stress-hormone-driven muscle-mass loss pre-competition (PDF p. 107, printed p. 96).

**Why it works** — Reduced total load is stated as the "principal condition" for reaching
supercompensation before competition (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95); the two things this
recovered state is then spent on — maximal-speed drills and sport-specific simulation — are
each chosen because their quality specifically depends on a well-rested nervous system and
energy-resource availability (maximal speed) or on the athlete's capacity to fully attend to
technical/tactical detail under simulated competitive stress (sport-specific tasks). Keeping
frequency similar while cutting volume is explicitly a quality lever, not a rest lever: more,
shorter, higher-quality sessions rather than fewer long ones.

**Why it works — Eric's baseline connection** — This entry gives explicit numeric structure
(volume down, frequency held, maximal-speed and sport-specific proportion up, 8-10 sessions/
week) to a taper logic that is not otherwise specified as a session-frequency rule anywhere in
`method-baseline.md`; the baseline's closest material is the general in-season rule "maintain
intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21), which agrees directionally (reduce volume,
don't reduce intensity/speed work) but does not specify a frequency-holding rule or an
explicit sport-specific-task ramp.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep:** the
week(s) immediately before a bowl game map most directly onto this framework — cut total
practice/lift volume hard, hold practice frequency roughly where it has been, shift the
practice mix toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavy game-plan (sport-specific)
simulation, and weight walkthroughs/individual work more than a normal week. **In-season
tuning week:** the standard in-season game week already functions as a compressed version of
this pattern (practice volume tapers toward the game, Thursday/Friday sessions shift toward
walkthrough-intensity techno-tactical work) — see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the specific team-sport
adaptation Issurin gives later in this chapter. **Season opener after fall camp:** the final
camp week before the opener is a pre-competitive microcycle relative to the whole camp block —
volume should come down from camp peak even though frequency (practice count) may stay similar.
The strength-during-taper disagreement Issurin reports (reduce high-resistance work vs. keep
sport-specific strength to protect force and prevent hormone-driven muscle loss) is directly
relevant to the recurring question of whether to lift heavy in bowl-prep week; this text does
not resolve it and presents both positions as live in the field.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Every numeric particular in Table 3.5 (frequency held at
8-10/week, "substantially reduced/increased" volume and speed contributions) is Issurin's own
applied synthesis with no cited dose-response study behind the specific numbers; he
acknowledges directly that "many contradictions exist regarding workout duration and frequency
of high intensity exercises" in the pre-competitive/taper literature generally (PDF p. 104,
printed p. 93, citing Kubukeli et al., 2002). **Population caveat:** the worked example
(Figure 3.7) and both named case examples (Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing morning scheduling;
swimmer/volleyball/tennis strength-reduction reports) are individual, dual, or non-contact
sports; none address a 100+ player roster with heterogeneous individual readiness, a fixed
practice-week structure set partly by NCAA rules, or the additional load of team walkthroughs
and special-teams reps that a football pre-competitive week must still include. The
"8-10 workouts per week" frequency figure assumes an individual/dual-sport training camp
structure and should not be read as a literal session-count target for a football bowl-prep
week. Issurin does not address game-week travel, opponent scouting load, or academic-calendar
constraints anywhere in this framework.

**Example** — A bowl-prep week could hold practice count similar to a normal in-season week
while cutting total practice/lift volume substantially, shifting a larger share of practice
time to explosive/speed work and full-speed game-plan simulation than a mid-season week would
carry, and deliberately expanding individual position-group time (film, technique correction)
relative to full-team periods — while treating the "how much to lift" question as an open
disagreement the source itself does not resolve, not a settled rule.

**Related** — [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging).

# A Two-Mini-Block Weekly Structure for In-Season Team Sports, Naming American Football Directly

**What it is** — Issurin addresses the specific constraint that team and dual sports (he
names **soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball** explicitly) run a 20-35 week season
where "the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is very limited"
(PDF pp. 108-109, printed pp. 97-98). He cites Fleck and Kraemer (1997): players typically
maintain strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks, after which strength variables
decrease dramatically. Because the usual one-week gap between games is too short to work
effectively on every training target (metabolic conditioning, maximal/explosive strength,
injury prevention, techno-tactical skill, game-specific endurance, active restoration) at once,
Issurin proposes adapting three BPC approaches at the *week* level: high concentration of
specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.
109, printed p. 98, "based on Baker, 2001" — a real cited source, not an uncited synthesis)
splits a standard Monday-Sunday week into two mini-blocks. **Mini-block 1 (Monday-Wednesday)**
targets sport-specific maximal and explosive strength as the dominant training aim: it opens
Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts**, combined with a medium-load
team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon).
This sequencing leaves **28-30 hours of recovery** after the strength key-workouts before
mini-block 2 begins, to let the anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.
**Mini-block 2 (Thursday-Saturday)** targets sport-specific team practice and immediate game
preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (intended to
deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session immediately
before the game itself (mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the specific forthcoming
opponent). Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
extra preparation — he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
ballistic explosive-type mesocycles to enhance jump performance instead.

**Why it works** — The mini-block structure is this chapter's direct answer to the constraint
stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs concentrated,
sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend competition long
enough to run full-length accumulation/transmutation/realization mesocycles
(see [[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] and
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]] for what those
normally require in duration). Splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,
each with its own key-workouts, is Issurin's way of keeping some of BPC's concentration
benefit even though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several.

**When to apply — this is the entry most directly answering the in-season half of the
strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`
pp.20-21), is compatible with and gets a concrete weekly shape from this framework: the
early-week mini-block is where intensity (maximal/explosive strength) gets its two key-workouts,
while the late-week mini-block is deliberately techno-tactical and load-restricted heading into
the game, which *is* the volume reduction the baseline rule calls for. The 28-30 hour recovery
window between the strength mini-block and the practice-heavy mini-block gives a specific,
citable number for how much gap a college program might target between its heaviest in-season
lift and the next high-intensity team session.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific day-by-day chart (Figure 3.8) is built from
one cited source, Baker (2001), a study of professional and college-aged rugby league players'
in-season concurrent training — a real, checkable citation, but a single study in a different
sport (rugby league) with a different weekly game/practice rhythm than college football
(which layers additional constraints: NCAA-mandated practice-time limits, travel, and a
Saturday-only game schedule rather than rugby league's varying weekly structure). **Population
caveat:** none of this section's evidence comes from American football itself — Issurin lists
football alongside soccer, rugby, and volleyball as sports the *problem* applies to, but the
worked example and its supporting citation are rugby-specific. **Inference:** the specific
"two key-workouts, 28-30 hours recovery" prescription should be treated as a structural
template to adapt to football's own practice-count and padded/unpadded-practice rules, not a
ready-made in-season lift schedule. Issurin gives no guidance here for bye weeks, short
(Thursday-game) weeks, or the postseason gap before a bowl game — those fall outside this
weekly-cycle framework and are closer to the pre-competitive/realization material in
[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]].

**Example** — A Baylor in-season week could place the two heaviest strength key-workouts on
Monday and Tuesday (following a Monday active-recovery/conditioning opener), hold Wednesday as
a conditioning-restorative bridge, then shift Thursday-Saturday entirely to team practice and
game-specific techno-tactical work, with the Friday or Saturday walkthrough load-restricted and
opponent-specific — checking that the strength work and the first hard team practice of
mini-block 2 are separated by at least a full day, per the 28-30 hour figure.

[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]],
[[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].
