# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
**5-7 days** — see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 89, printed p. 78) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.

**Why it works** — Issurin frames the point-scale quantification (adapted from the 5-point
load scale) as serving three purposes: it lets coaches in non-measurable sports (sailing,
team/dual sports) express load numerically and visually; it lets athletes see and
consciously anticipate key-workouts and the restoration that follows load peaks
(a didactic use); and it lets whole microcycles be compared to each other for planning
purposes (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp. 80-81). The peak/trough pattern itself follows the same
general logic as [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]: concentrating the
week's hardest sessions into one, two, or three peaks (rather than spreading maximal effort
evenly across every day) lets fatigue clear between peaks so each peak can still be
performed at a high standard.

**When to apply** — Classifying a week's purpose before assigning workouts to it (is this
week meant to adjust athletes to new load, develop fitness, deliver an extreme stimulus, tune
for competition, compete, or actively recover), and then shaping that week's daily load curve
around one, two, or three peaks depending on athlete level and the week's targeted abilities.
**Inference, mapped to a college football calendar:** early fall camp days function like
Issurin's **adjustment** microcycle (medium load, gradual ramp, until two-a-days are
tolerated); the heaviest camp week(s) resemble the **impact** type (very high-extreme load,
short duration, 4-7 days — matching the "impact week" concept sometimes used informally in
strength-staff planning); the week of the season opener and each bowl-prep week function as
**pre-competitive** microcycles (see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]]); a
normal in-season game week is Issurin's **competitive** microcycle in form (the whole week
organized around one **competition**, 2-7 days), though its internal training content is
closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye
week or the week after a game before a short turnaround functions as a **restoration**
microcycle. **Eric's baseline** does not currently name these six categories explicitly, but
the general planning language ("a 'training week' does not have to equal 7 calendar days,"
`method-baseline.md`, "Periodization and programming," citing week1-lecture.md p.39) is
consistent with treating microcycle type, not just calendar week, as the planning unit.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The six-type table's specific duration ranges are
Issurin's own applied categorization; no citation or derivation is given for why, e.g., the
loading type is 5-9 days rather than some other range. **Inference:** none of the six types
or the one-/two-/three-peak wave figures are demonstrated on a team-sport example in this
section (that comes later, 3.1.7); the load-wave figures here are drawn from individual/dual
sport contexts, and the specific number-of-peaks guidance ("one-peak... not [for] novice and
less prepared athletes") is stated for individual-sport training loads, not validated for a
100+ player roster with heterogeneous training ages. The point-scale system inherits every
limitation already logged for the underlying RPE/restoration-time scale in
[[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (subjective, no cited validation
of the specific cut-points).

**Example** — A four-week fall-camp block could be read as adjustment (days 1-5, single
practices, medium load) into loading (days 6-14, one-a-days plus early two-a-days) into an
impact microcycle (the hardest stretch of two-a-days, 4-7 days) into a pre-competitive
microcycle in the week before the opener — each transition marked by a deliberate change in
purpose and load level, not just a generic "camp is getting harder" narrative.

**Related** — [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]] (the 5-point scale
this section's point-quantification is built on), [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]],
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]].

# Six Microcycle Types by Purpose and Load, With One-, Two-, and Three-Peak Weekly Load Waves

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (PDF p. 88, printed p. 77; verified against the page image)
gives six microcycle types, each with a stated purpose, load level, design particular, and
duration range: **Adjustment** (initial adaptation to loads, medium load, gradual workload
increase, **5-7 days**); **Loading** (fitness development, substantial-high load, big/substantial
workloads, **5-9 days**); **Impact** (fitness development via extreme stimuli, very
high-extreme load, summation of extreme workloads, **4-7 days**); **Pre-competitive**
(immediate preparation for competition, medium load, tuning with event-specific means,
**5-7 days**, see [[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] for full detail);
**Competitive** (participation in competition, high-very high load, sport/event-specific
performance, **2-7 days**); **Restoration** (active recovery, low load, wide spectrum of
restorative means, **3-7 days**). Issurin notes the adjustment microcycle can shorten to
3-5 days mid-season (e.g., starting a new training stage or a camp), and the restoration
microcycle after camp or competition typically runs 3-4 days mid-season (PDF p. 88, printed
p. 77). Separately, Issurin describes load variation **within** a microcycle as a "wave-shape
design" using the 5-point load scale from [[framework--workout-load-classification-and-rpe-mapping]]:
Figure 3.1 (PDF p. 90, printed p. 79) shows one-, two-, and three-peak weekly load patterns
for single-workout-per-day microcycles. Two- and three-peak designs are described as "used
most widely" because they let athletes handle a relatively large weekly workload with reduced
excessive-fatigue risk; the one-peak design concentrates several developmental workouts for a
"more profound and stressful training response," a pattern reserved for "sufficiently
prepared high-performance athletes" and not for novices. For microcycles with two workouts
per day, Figure 3.2 (PDF p. 91, printed p. 80) gives a worked ten-workout example: two
development workouts open the week (first peak), two medium-load supporting workouts
provide restoration, then a three-session mini-block including two key-workouts forms the
second peak, with the week's final session usable as a time-trial or scrimmage.

performed at a high standard.

closer to what [[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] describes; and a bye

# Popov's Aerobic Microcycle: Anaerobic Glycolytic Work Is Nearly Absent Even for a 100m Freestyle Sprinter

**What it is** — Issurin presents Alexander Popov's (Russia, multi-Olympic/World 50-100m
Freestyle swimming champion) typical strength-aerobic microcycle from his preparatory phase
(the accumulation mesocycle, in Block Periodization terms) as an example (PDF pp. 92-94,
printed pp. 81-83, Figure 3.3 and Table 3.2; sourced to "courtesy of Gennadi Touretski,
personal communication," Popov's coach). Across ten workouts, anaerobic threshold (AT) work
and technical stroke-count drills dominated; maximal-speed (alactic) exercises appeared daily
in medium proportions; aerobic power (AP) work appeared in only three workouts; strength
endurance (speed-resisted) drills were a large contributor; and anaerobic glycolytic (AnG)
work appeared **once**, in a 200m stepwise all-out time trial. Issurin's three stated
takeaways: (a) even for a prominent sprinter, aerobic-endurance volume is very high in this
microcycle; (b) strength can be developed effectively through force accentuation inside
sport-specific drills rather than only in the weight room; (c) despite 100m Freestyle's high
metabolic reliance on anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity, glycolytic *training* volume in
this aerobic microcycle is negligible — reserved instead for the anaerobic microcycle (see
[[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]]). Table 3.2 (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84)
lists the compatible secondary modalities for an aerobic microcycle: maximum strength (first
priority; combining aerobic and strength work "ensures better oxidation in enlarged
muscles"), anaerobic alactic/maximum speed (sprints "break monotony and activate a wide
spectrum of muscle fibers... exploited in subsequent aerobic workloads"), aerobic
strength-endurance (speed-resisted exercises), and movement technique (drilled during
prolonged aerobic work without aggravating metabolic adaptation). Issurin adds a specific
timing rule: strength work should not follow directly after exhaustive aerobic training,
because the testosterone/cortisol ratio needed for protein synthesis stays depressed for
"many hours" post-endurance-work (Viru, Karelson & Smirnova, 1992); **24 hours** of recovery,
with only low-level loads in between, is stated as the needed gap (PDF p. 95, printed p. 84,
citing Chesley et al., 1992 for protein-turnover persisting ≥24 hours post-resistance-work).

**Why it works** — Issurin's own stated mechanism for combining aerobic and strength work is
that concurrent aerobic stimulus improves oxidative support in the muscle mass strength
training builds, addressing the problem (raised in Chapter 1's swimmer interference case,
[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]]) that strength-built muscle mass
without matched aerobic enzyme/mitochondrial development doesn't help endurance-sport
performance. The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic sequencing rule follows directly from the
testosterone/cortisol citation: an anabolic hormonal environment is a precondition for the
strength stimulus to "take," and that environment is temporarily suppressed right after
exhaustive endurance work.

**When to apply** — Designing an aerobic-base microcycle (early accumulation mesocycle, see
[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]]) for any athlete needing both an
aerobic base and strength, and specifically the 24-hour strength-after-aerobic spacing rule
whenever a hard conditioning session and a strength session are close together in the same
microcycle. **Inference:** for football specifically, this example argues against treating
"conditioning day" and "lift day" as interchangeable slots without checking the sequencing
gap, particularly early in an off-season aerobic-base block.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite swimmer's program, reported
secondhand by his personal coach with no comparison data and no other athletes' programs
shown; it is Issurin's chosen illustrative anecdote, not a study. **Inference:** swimming's
metabolic and technical demands (continuous, cyclical, non-contact, highly technique-limited)
differ substantially from football; the specific finding that glycolytic training is nearly
absent in this microcycle should not be read as "football conditioning should minimize
glycolytic work" — Eric's baseline's own stated fall-camp priority stack treats glycolytic
conditioning as something to "absorb incidentally through camp and practice" rather than
program directly (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing
`class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39), which is a different reason (practical prioritization under a
tight camp calendar) than Popov's reason (protecting a compatible-modality structure within
one microcycle type). The 24-hour strength-after-aerobic figure rests on two cited studies
(Viru et al. 1992; Chesley et al. 1992) not detailed further in this text — treat the
direction as supported but the exact "24 hours" as an applied rule of thumb, not a
precisely-dosed threshold verified here.

**Example** — A Baylor off-season aerobic-base week could sequence a hard aerobic-threshold
run or bike session on Monday, hold Tuesday's strength session to low-intensity technique
work only, and place the next true max-strength session on Wednesday (roughly 48 hours after
Monday's endurance work), rather than programming a hard conditioning session the evening
before a heavy squat day.

**Related** — [[framework--anaerobic-glycolytic-microcycle-design]],
[[case-study--concurrent-training-interference-and-decay]],
[[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# The Anaerobic Glycolytic Microcycle Trades Restoration for Fatigue-Tolerant, Lactate-Driven Development

**What it is** — Issurin describes the microcycle that forms the content of the transmutation
mesocycle (PDF pp. 97-100, printed pp. 86-89, Table 3.3 and Figure 3.5). Its compatible
modalities (Table 3.3): **strength endurance** (mostly anaerobic; high-resistance drills
inside regular workouts or separate sessions; produces a dual strength-endurance and
anaerobic-metabolism effect), **anaerobic alactic/maximal speed** (used by moderately fatigued
athletes since a well-restored state is usually unavailable here; sprints add diversity and
short-duration power contribution), **low-intensity aerobic exercise** (used throughout as
active restoration, alongside stretching/relaxation), and **movement technique/tactics** (given
prime placement and treated as essential despite metabolic fatigue, because competition itself
imposes comparable fatigue on technique). Issurin gives specific lactate-based intensity
zones: workloads producing **5-8 mM** blood lactate improve maximal aerobic power and
aerobic-anaerobic interaction and are more typical early-to-mid-season; workloads above
**8 mM** target anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity specifically and dominate in the final
weeks before the target competition (PDF pp. 97-98, printed pp. 86-87). The worked ten-workout
chart (Figure 3.5, PDF p. 100, printed p. 89) uses a three-peak load design with six
development workouts (three of them key-workouts) targeting anaerobic glycolytic power,
anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength endurance, buffered by a mid-week restoration
"window" (Wednesday evening) and two medium-load alactic-maintenance sessions.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the defining feature of this microcycle is fatigue
accumulation with insufficient restoration by design (PDF p. 99, printed p. 88): high-load
glycolytic work drives maximal heart rate/cardiac output, maximal oxygen deficit/debt and
blood lactate accumulation, plus a rise in catecholamines and cortisol with testosterone
suppressed for 24+ hours (citing Viru, 1995). At a workout frequency of 6-12 sessions/week,
fatigue accumulation across the microcycle is "inevitable" — the design goal is to manage that
fatigue (through workout sequencing, deliberately-placed restoration, and monitoring) rather
than to avoid it, which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one.

**When to apply** — Structuring the highest-intensity block of a transmutation mesocycle
(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) when the
targeted abilities are anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity and anaerobic-component strength
endurance. Issurin's four stated guidelines for managing the built-in fatigue (PDF p. 99,
printed p. 88): sequence development workouts with expected fatigue accumulation in mind;
treat restoration workouts as a planned, non-optional part of the week; use active
restoration means (stretching, low-intensity drills, massage, physiotherapy, nutritional
support); and prioritize training-response monitoring here specifically. **Inference:** this
maps to the hardest week(s) of fall camp or a mid-season "gut check" conditioning emphasis,
where the department accepts several days of accumulating fatigue in exchange for a
concentrated glycolytic-capacity stimulus, rather than trying to keep every day fresh.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific lactate cut-points (5-8 mM vs. >8 mM) and
the 6-12 workouts/week frequency figure are presented without a cited validation study in this
passage; treat them as Issurin's own applied heuristics. **Inference:** none of this section's
evidence is football-specific — it is framed around individual/dual sports and combat sports
with a season structure that tolerates a dedicated multi-day high-fatigue block, which is
harder to fit inside a single football in-season week (see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the team-sport-adapted version).
**Eric's baseline** explicitly treats glycolytic conditioning for football as something to
absorb incidentally through camp and practice rather than as a primary programmed target
(`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md` pp.34, 39)
— a different posture than this microcycle's deliberate, concentrated glycolytic emphasis,
which is drawn from individual/dual/combat-sport programming. Blood lactate testing
capability (needed to hit the stated mM zones precisely) is not a standard part of the
department's documented testing stack per this baseline corpus.

**Example** — A transmutation-mesocycle week built for a combat-sport or team-sport athlete
needing anaerobic capacity could place two key-workouts (Monday and Thursday, per Figure 3.5's
pattern) targeting >8 mM glycolytic capacity work, a Tuesday alactic-maintenance session, a
Wednesday evening restoration window, and Friday/Saturday sessions blending anaerobic
glycolytic power with strength endurance — accepting that athletes will not be fully
restored entering most of these sessions.

**Related** — [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]],
[[principle--training-modality-compatibility-in-a-workout]].

# The Anaerobic Glycolytic Microcycle Trades Restoration for Fatigue-Tolerant, Lactate-Driven Development

**What it is** — Issurin describes the microcycle that forms the content of the transmutation
mesocycle (PDF pp. 97-100, printed pp. 86-89, Table 3.3 and Figure 3.5). Its compatible
modalities (Table 3.3): **strength endurance** (mostly anaerobic; high-resistance drills
inside regular workouts or separate sessions; produces a dual strength-endurance and
anaerobic-metabolism effect), **anaerobic alactic/maximal speed** (used by moderately fatigued
athletes since a well-restored state is usually unavailable here; sprints add diversity and
short-duration power contribution), **low-intensity aerobic exercise** (used throughout as
active restoration, alongside stretching/relaxation), and **movement technique/tactics** (given
prime placement and treated as essential despite metabolic fatigue, because competition itself
imposes comparable fatigue on technique). Issurin gives specific lactate-based intensity
zones: workloads producing **5-8 mM** blood lactate improve maximal aerobic power and
aerobic-anaerobic interaction and are more typical early-to-mid-season; workloads above
**8 mM** target anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity specifically and dominate in the final
weeks before the target competition (PDF pp. 97-98, printed pp. 86-87). The worked ten-workout
chart (Figure 3.5, PDF p. 100, printed p. 89) uses a three-peak load design with six
development workouts (three of them key-workouts) targeting anaerobic glycolytic power,
anaerobic glycolytic capacity, and strength endurance, buffered by a mid-week restoration
"window" (Wednesday evening) and two medium-load alactic-maintenance sessions.

**Why it works** — Issurin states the defining feature of this microcycle is fatigue
accumulation with insufficient restoration by design (PDF p. 99, printed p. 88): high-load
glycolytic work drives maximal heart rate/cardiac output, maximal oxygen deficit/debt and
blood lactate accumulation, plus a rise in catecholamines and cortisol with testosterone
suppressed for 24+ hours (citing Viru, 1995). At a workout frequency of 6-12 sessions/week,
fatigue accumulation across the microcycle is "inevitable": the design goal is to manage that
fatigue (through workout sequencing, deliberately-placed restoration, and monitoring) rather
than to avoid it, which is what distinguishes this microcycle from the aerobic one.

**When to apply** — Structuring the highest-intensity block of a transmutation mesocycle
(see [[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]]) when the
targeted abilities are anaerobic glycolytic power/capacity and anaerobic-component strength
endurance. Issurin's four stated guidelines for managing the built-in fatigue (PDF p. 99,
printed p. 88): sequence development workouts with expected fatigue accumulation in mind;
treat restoration workouts as a planned, non-optional part of the week; use active
restoration means (stretching, low-intensity drills, massage, physiotherapy, nutritional
support); and prioritize training-response monitoring here specifically. **Inference:** this
maps to the hardest week(s) of fall camp or a mid-season "gut check" conditioning emphasis,
where the department accepts several days of accumulating fatigue in exchange for a
concentrated glycolytic-capacity stimulus, rather than trying to keep every day fresh.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific lactate cut-points (5-8 mM vs. >8 mM) and
the 6-12 workouts/week frequency figure are presented without a cited validation study in this
passage; treat them as Issurin's own applied heuristics. **Inference:** none of this section's

with a season structure that tolerates a dedicated multi-day high-fatigue block, which is

restored entering most of these sessions.

# Sedykh's Hammer-Throw Microcycle Puts Explosive Strength Only in Morning, Fresh-Athlete Sessions

**What it is** — Issurin presents the eleven-workout microcycle of two-time Olympic champion
hammer thrower Yuri Sedykh (USSR), as reported by his coach (Bondarchuk, 1986) (PDF pp.
101-103, printed pp. 90-92, Table 3.4 and Figure 3.6). Four essential features: (a)
event-specific explosive-strength exercises (throwing different-weight hammers), the
top-priority target, appear **exclusively** in morning sessions and always in the **initial**
part of the workout, to use the athlete's most favorable physical state for the key-exercise;
(b) maximum-strength exercises (barbell snatch, half squats, good mornings), a supporting
role, are placed in five sessions — four separate evening sessions plus once in the second
part of a morning session; (c) additional explosive-strength work (standing jumps) appears
three times, but never when the athlete is in his best condition, i.e., placed after the
primary explosive work is already done; (d) restorative activity (basketball, swimming,
stretching) is built into the program, including on the day off. Issurin separately cites a
related mechanism study: Cardinale and Stone (2006) measured resting blood testosterone and
countermovement vertical jump in 70 elite athletes (48 men, 22 women; sprinters, handball,
volleyball, soccer) after a 10-hour fast and a rest day, finding a significant positive
relationship between testosterone and jump height (r = 0.61, p < 0.001) (PDF p. 103, printed
p. 92). Issurin's own stated implications from that study: athletes with relatively high
testosterone (either sex) have some inherited predisposition for explosive-strength
performance, and microcycle design for explosive-strength development should avoid excessive
fatigue, because fatigue suppresses testosterone and sharply reduces the training effect of
maximal-power exercises.

**Why it works** — Issurin's stated mechanism (PDF pp. 92-93, printed pp. 92-93 [sic, both
appear on the same printed page 92]) is that explosive strength depends on the sensitivity
and reactivity of the neuromuscular system, and excessive fatigue "disrupts the subtle
regulation of neural input and muscle contraction"; testosterone is named as the hormone
determining strength training's anabolic effect and as an index of induced physical stress
(Viru and Viru, 2000). **Inference:** the placement rule (explosive work only when fresh,
morning, first in the session) follows directly from this same logic already generalized in
[[heuristic--exercise-sequencing-by-fatigue-state]] — CNS-dependent, high-precision qualities
need a well-rested athlete — this case study is simply that general rule applied to one
specific, historically documented program.

**When to apply** — As a concrete illustration of sequencing explosive/technical power work
at the very start of a session, before any fatigue-inducing supporting work, for athletes
whose primary target ability is explosive strength in a highly coordinated skill.
**Inference:** in football, this maps most directly to skill-position or specialist
explosive-power development (e.g., jump-training or Olympic-lift-variant work meant to
transfer to explosive movement) — placing that work first in a session, before conditioning
or high-volume accessory work, mirrors Sedykh's morning-first placement of hammer throws.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is a single elite thrower's program from a single
coach's secondhand report (Bondarchuk, 1986), with no comparison athlete or outcome data
beyond the general BPC narrative already logged in
[[case-study--bondarchuk-hammer-throw-block-mesocycles]] — it illustrates a design principle,
not a validated dose-response result. **Inference:** hammer throw is an acyclic, single-effort,
highly technical power event with no contact and no in-competition fatigue accumulation across
a "game," unlike football; the specific workout counts, throw counts, and session splits in
Table 3.4 should not be copied as a template. The testosterone-jump correlation (Cardinale and
Stone, 2006) is cross-sectional and observational (r = 0.61 explains well under half the
variance in jump height) — it identifies an association at one time point in rested athletes,
not a training intervention; it does not establish that raising testosterone directly causes
higher jump performance, only that they covary. Population also spans track, handball,
volleyball and soccer athletes of both sexes, not football specifically.

**Example** — A football skill player's Tuesday lift built around explosive-power development
(e.g., trap-bar jumps, medicine-ball throws) should be sequenced first in the session, on a day
following adequate rest, with any high-volume or fatiguing accessory work placed afterward —
not the reverse.

14	# The Pre-Competitive Microcycle: Cut Volume Hard, Raise Maximal-Speed and Sport-Specific Work, Keep Frequency
15	
16	**What it is** — The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization
17	mesocycle (see [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]) and is also called the
18	taper at the microcycle level (PDF pp. 104-105, printed pp. 93-94; verified against page
19	images). It must satisfy three demands (PDF p. 104, printed p. 93): sport-specific
20	exercises/tasks that simulate the forthcoming competition and build mental readiness and
21	toughness; development of maximal speed/power and sport-specific quickness; and full (or
22	partial) restoration after the preceding transmutation mesocycle's fatiguing workloads. Table
23	3.5 (PDF p. 105, printed p. 94, verified against page image) gives seven prescriptive
24	characteristics: **workload volume** — substantially reduced, to create conditions for full
25	recovery; **volume of intense exercises specifically** — substantially reduced versus the
26	prior mesocycle, so total drill volume falls but quality rises; **contribution of maximum
27	speed/power exercises** — substantially **increased** (well-rested athletes respond better to
28	maximal-speed drills, and maximal-speed training residuals are the shortest of any ability, per
29	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]); **contribution of
30	sport-specific tasks** — substantially increased (simulative tasks improve adaptation to
31	expected competitive stressors); **workout frequency** — usually kept **similar** to the
32	previous mesocycle (subdividing the same total work into more, smaller portions raises
33	quality per session even as volume falls); **organization** — a rational mix of group,
34	individual and mixed workouts, weighted somewhat more toward individual work than usual, so
35	athletes can attend to personal technical detail and coach rapport; **restoration** —
36	deliberately favorable conditions and an increased volume of restorative exercises/workouts,
37	since athletes have more free time and motivation to use it. Issurin states that in qualified
38	athletes, especially during a pre-competitive training camp, maintaining frequency in practice
39	means **eight to ten workouts per week** even as volume per workout drops (PDF p. 105, printed
40	p. 94). Workout timing should match the expected competition's daily biological-rhythm window
41	(example given: Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing regattas run only in the morning, so pre-Olympic
42	training is scheduled to place peak-effort sessions at that same morning time, PDF p. 106,
43	printed p. 95). Figure 3.7 (PDF p. 107, printed p. 96) gives a worked chart for a
44	morning-peak-performance pre-competitive microcycle, alternating maximum-strength/technique
45	mornings with sport-specific-simulation/alactic afternoons, moving toward heavier
46	sport-specific-simulation and explosive-strength content later in the week. On strength work
47	specifically, Issurin notes a real disagreement in the field: many athletes (particularly
48	swimmers, per Platonov & Fesenko, 1990, and also reported among volleyball and tennis players)
49	report high-resistance work pre-competition degrades fine technical skill, arguing for
50	reducing or excluding it; but sport-specific maximal/explosive strength work is also argued to
51	maintain the technical force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and to prevent uncontrolled,
52	stress-hormone-driven muscle-mass loss pre-competition (PDF p. 107, printed p. 96).
53	
54	**Why it works** — Reduced total load is stated as the "principal condition" for reaching
55	supercompensation before competition (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95); the two things this
56	recovered state is then spent on — maximal-speed drills and sport-specific simulation — are
57	each chosen because their quality specifically depends on a well-rested nervous system and
58	energy-resource availability (maximal speed) or on the athlete's capacity to fully attend to
59	technical/tactical detail under simulated competitive stress (sport-specific tasks). Keeping
60	frequency similar while cutting volume is explicitly a quality lever, not a rest lever: more,
61	shorter, higher-quality sessions rather than fewer long ones.
62	
63	**Why it works — Eric's baseline connection** — This entry gives explicit numeric structure
64	(volume down, frequency held, maximal-speed and sport-specific proportion up, 8-10 sessions/
65	week) to a taper logic that is not otherwise specified as a session-frequency rule anywhere in
66	`method-baseline.md`; the baseline's closest material is the general in-season rule "maintain
67	intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
68	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21), which agrees directionally (reduce volume,
69	don't reduce intensity/speed work) but does not specify a frequency-holding rule or an
70	explicit sport-specific-task ramp.
71	
72	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep:** the
73	week(s) immediately before a bowl game map most directly onto this framework — cut total
74	practice/lift volume hard, hold practice frequency roughly where it has been, shift the
75	practice mix toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavy game-plan (sport-specific)
76	simulation, and weight walkthroughs/individual work more than a normal week. **In-season
77	tuning week:** the standard in-season game week already functions as a compressed version of
78	this pattern (practice volume tapers toward the game, Thursday/Friday sessions shift toward
79	walkthrough-intensity techno-tactical work) — see
80	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the specific team-sport
81	adaptation Issurin gives later in this chapter. **Season opener after fall camp:** the final
82	camp week before the opener is a pre-competitive microcycle relative to the whole camp block —
83	volume should come down from camp peak even though frequency (practice count) may stay similar.
84	The strength-during-taper disagreement Issurin reports (reduce high-resistance work vs. keep
85	sport-specific strength to protect force and prevent hormone-driven muscle loss) is directly
86	relevant to the recurring question of whether to lift heavy in bowl-prep week; this text does
87	not resolve it and presents both positions as live in the field.
88	
89	**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Every numeric particular in Table 3.5 (frequency held at
90	8-10/week, "substantially reduced/increased" volume and speed contributions) is Issurin's own
91	applied synthesis with no cited dose-response study behind the specific numbers; he
92	acknowledges directly that "many contradictions exist regarding workout duration and frequency
93	of high intensity exercises" in the pre-competitive/taper literature generally (PDF p. 104,
94	printed p. 93, citing Kubukeli et al., 2002). **Population caveat:** the worked example
95	(Figure 3.7) and both named case examples (Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing morning scheduling;
96	swimmer/volleyball/tennis strength-reduction reports) are individual, dual, or non-contact
97	sports; none address a 100+ player roster with heterogeneous individual readiness, a fixed
98	practice-week structure set partly by NCAA rules, or the additional load of team walkthroughs
99	and special-teams reps that a football pre-competitive week must still include. The
100	"8-10 workouts per week" frequency figure assumes an individual/dual-sport training camp
101	structure and should not be read as a literal session-count target for a football bowl-prep
102	week. Issurin does not address game-week travel, opponent scouting load, or academic-calendar
103	constraints anywhere in this framework.
104	
105	**Example** — A bowl-prep week could hold practice count similar to a normal in-season week
106	while cutting total practice/lift volume substantially, shifting a larger share of practice
107	time to explosive/speed work and full-speed game-plan simulation than a mid-season week would
108	carry, and deliberately expanding individual position-group time (film, technique correction)
109	relative to full-team periods — while treating the "how much to lift" question as an open
110	disagreement the source itself does not resolve, not a settled rule.
111	
112	**Related** — [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]],
113	[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
114	[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
115	[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
116	[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging).

# The Pre-Competitive Microcycle: Cut Volume Hard, Raise Maximal-Speed and Sport-Specific Work, Keep Frequency

**What it is** — The pre-competitive microcycle forms the content of the realization
mesocycle (see [[framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]]) and is also called the
taper at the microcycle level (PDF pp. 104-105, printed pp. 93-94; verified against page
images). It must satisfy three demands (PDF p. 104, printed p. 93): sport-specific
exercises/tasks that simulate the forthcoming competition and build mental readiness and
toughness; development of maximal speed/power and sport-specific quickness; and full (or
partial) restoration after the preceding transmutation mesocycle's fatiguing workloads. Table
3.5 (PDF p. 105, printed p. 94, verified against page image) gives seven prescriptive
characteristics: **workload volume** — substantially reduced, to create conditions for full
recovery; **volume of intense exercises specifically** — substantially reduced versus the
prior mesocycle, so total drill volume falls but quality rises; **contribution of maximum
speed/power exercises** — substantially **increased** (well-rested athletes respond better to
maximal-speed drills, and maximal-speed training residuals are the shortest of any ability, per
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]); **contribution of
sport-specific tasks** — substantially increased (simulative tasks improve adaptation to
expected competitive stressors); **workout frequency** — usually kept **similar** to the
previous mesocycle (subdividing the same total work into more, smaller portions raises
quality per session even as volume falls); **organization** — a rational mix of group,
individual and mixed workouts, weighted somewhat more toward individual work than usual, so
athletes can attend to personal technical detail and coach rapport; **restoration** —
deliberately favorable conditions and an increased volume of restorative exercises/workouts,
since athletes have more free time and motivation to use it. Issurin states that in qualified
athletes, especially during a pre-competitive training camp, maintaining frequency in practice
means **eight to ten workouts per week** even as volume per workout drops (PDF p. 105, printed
p. 94). Workout timing should match the expected competition's daily biological-rhythm window
(example given: Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing regattas run only in the morning, so pre-Olympic
training is scheduled to place peak-effort sessions at that same morning time, PDF p. 106,
printed p. 95). Figure 3.7 (PDF p. 107, printed p. 96) gives a worked chart for a
morning-peak-performance pre-competitive microcycle, alternating maximum-strength/technique
mornings with sport-specific-simulation/alactic afternoons, moving toward heavier
sport-specific-simulation and explosive-strength content later in the week. On strength work
specifically, Issurin notes a real disagreement in the field: many athletes (particularly
swimmers, per Platonov & Fesenko, 1990, and also reported among volleyball and tennis players)
report high-resistance work pre-competition degrades fine technical skill, arguing for
reducing or excluding it; but sport-specific maximal/explosive strength work is also argued to
maintain the technical force component (Bompa & Carrera, 2003) and to prevent uncontrolled,
stress-hormone-driven muscle-mass loss pre-competition (PDF p. 107, printed p. 96).

**Why it works** — Reduced total load is stated as the "principal condition" for reaching
supercompensation before competition (PDF p. 106, printed p. 95); the two things this
recovered state is then spent on — maximal-speed drills and sport-specific simulation — are
each chosen because their quality specifically depends on a well-rested nervous system and
energy-resource availability (maximal speed) or on the athlete's capacity to fully attend to
technical/tactical detail under simulated competitive stress (sport-specific tasks). Keeping
frequency similar while cutting volume is explicitly a quality lever, not a rest lever: more,
shorter, higher-quality sessions rather than fewer long ones.

**Why it works — Eric's baseline connection** — This entry gives explicit numeric structure
(volume down, frequency held, maximal-speed and sport-specific proportion up, 8-10 sessions/
week) to a taper logic that is not otherwise specified as a session-frequency rule anywhere in
`method-baseline.md`; the baseline's closest material is the general in-season rule "maintain
intensity, reduce volume" (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md` pp.20-21), which agrees directionally (reduce volume,
don't reduce intensity/speed work) but does not specify a frequency-holding rule or an
explicit sport-specific-task ramp.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Bowl prep:** the
week(s) immediately before a bowl game map most directly onto this framework — cut total
practice/lift volume hard, hold practice frequency roughly where it has been, shift the
practice mix toward maximal-speed/explosive work and heavy game-plan (sport-specific)
simulation, and weight walkthroughs/individual work more than a normal week. **In-season
tuning week:** the standard in-season game week already functions as a compressed version of
this pattern (practice volume tapers toward the game, Thursday/Friday sessions shift toward
walkthrough-intensity techno-tactical work) — see
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]] for the specific team-sport
adaptation Issurin gives later in this chapter. **Season opener after fall camp:** the final
camp week before the opener is a pre-competitive microcycle relative to the whole camp block —
volume should come down from camp peak even though frequency (practice count) may stay similar.
The strength-during-taper disagreement Issurin reports (reduce high-resistance work vs. keep
sport-specific strength to protect force and prevent hormone-driven muscle loss) is directly
relevant to the recurring question of whether to lift heavy in bowl-prep week; this text does
not resolve it and presents both positions as live in the field.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — Every numeric particular in Table 3.5 (frequency held at
8-10/week, "substantially reduced/increased" volume and speed contributions) is Issurin's own
applied synthesis with no cited dose-response study behind the specific numbers; he
acknowledges directly that "many contradictions exist regarding workout duration and frequency
of high intensity exercises" in the pre-competitive/taper literature generally (PDF p. 104,
printed p. 93, citing Kubukeli et al., 2002). **Population caveat:** the worked example
(Figure 3.7) and both named case examples (Olympic canoe-kayak/rowing morning scheduling;
swimmer/volleyball/tennis strength-reduction reports) are individual, dual, or non-contact
sports; none address a 100+ player roster with heterogeneous individual readiness, a fixed
practice-week structure set partly by NCAA rules, or the additional load of team walkthroughs
and special-teams reps that a football pre-competitive week must still include. The
"8-10 workouts per week" frequency figure assumes an individual/dual-sport training camp
structure and should not be read as a literal session-count target for a football bowl-prep
week. Issurin does not address game-week travel, opponent scouting load, or academic-calendar
constraints anywhere in this framework.

**Example** — A bowl-prep week could hold practice count similar to a normal in-season week
while cutting total practice/lift volume substantially, shifting a larger share of practice
time to explosive/speed work and full-speed game-plan simulation than a mid-season week would
carry, and deliberately expanding individual position-group time (film, technique correction)
relative to full-team periods — while treating the "how much to lift" question as an open
disagreement the source itself does not resolve, not a settled rule.

[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
[[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--fitness-fatigue-modeling-and-taper-timing]] (staging).

# A Two-Mini-Block Weekly Structure for In-Season Team Sports, Naming American Football Directly

**What it is** — Issurin addresses the specific constraint that team and dual sports (he
names **soccer, American football, rugby, volleyball** explicitly) run a 20-35 week season
where "the possibility of inserting highly concentrated training blocks is very limited"
(PDF pp. 108-109, printed pp. 97-98). He cites Fleck and Kraemer (1997): players typically
maintain strength near pre-season levels for 14-16 weeks, after which strength variables
decrease dramatically. Because the usual one-week gap between games is too short to work
effectively on every training target (metabolic conditioning, maximal/explosive strength,
injury prevention, techno-tactical skill, game-specific endurance, active restoration) at once,
Issurin proposes adapting three BPC approaches at the *week* level: high concentration of
specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.
109, printed p. 98, "based on Baker, 2001" — a real cited source, not an uncited synthesis)
splits a standard Monday-Sunday week into two mini-blocks. **Mini-block 1 (Monday-Wednesday)**
targets sport-specific maximal and explosive strength as the dominant training aim: it opens
Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts**, combined with a medium-load
team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon).
This sequencing leaves **28-30 hours of recovery** after the strength key-workouts before
mini-block 2 begins, to let the anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.
**Mini-block 2 (Thursday-Saturday)** targets sport-specific team practice and immediate game
preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (intended to
deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session immediately
before the game itself (mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the specific forthcoming
opponent). Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
extra preparation — he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
ballistic explosive-type mesocycles to enhance jump performance instead.

**Why it works** — The mini-block structure is this chapter's direct answer to the constraint
stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs concentrated,
sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend competition long
enough to run full-length accumulation/transmutation/realization mesocycles
(see [[framework--accumulation-mesocycle-duration-and-monitoring]] and
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]] for what those
normally require in duration). Splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,
each with its own key-workouts, is Issurin's way of keeping some of BPC's concentration
benefit even though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several.

**When to apply — this is the entry most directly answering the in-season half of the
strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`
pp.20-21), is compatible with and gets a concrete weekly shape from this framework: the
early-week mini-block is where intensity (maximal/explosive strength) gets its two key-workouts,
while the late-week mini-block is deliberately techno-tactical and load-restricted heading into
the game, which *is* the volume reduction the baseline rule calls for. The 28-30 hour recovery
window between the strength mini-block and the practice-heavy mini-block gives a specific,
citable number for how much gap a college program might target between its heaviest in-season
lift and the next high-intensity team session.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The specific day-by-day chart (Figure 3.8) is built from
one cited source, Baker (2001), a study of professional and college-aged rugby league players'
in-season concurrent training — a real, checkable citation, but a single study in a different
sport (rugby league) with a different weekly game/practice rhythm than college football
(which layers additional constraints: NCAA-mandated practice-time limits, travel, and a
Saturday-only game schedule rather than rugby league's varying weekly structure). **Population
caveat:** none of this section's evidence comes from American football itself — Issurin lists
football alongside soccer, rugby, and volleyball as sports the *problem* applies to, but the
worked example and its supporting citation are rugby-specific. **Inference:** the specific
"two key-workouts, 28-30 hours recovery" prescription should be treated as a structural
template to adapt to football's own practice-count and padded/unpadded-practice rules, not a
ready-made in-season lift schedule. Issurin gives no guidance here for bye weeks, short
(Thursday-game) weeks, or the postseason gap before a bowl game — those fall outside this
weekly-cycle framework and are closer to the pre-competitive/realization material in
[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]] and
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]].

**Example** — A Baylor in-season week could place the two heaviest strength key-workouts on
Monday and Tuesday (following a Monday active-recovery/conditioning opener), hold Wednesday as
a conditioning-restorative bridge, then shift Thursday-Saturday entirely to team practice and
game-specific techno-tactical work, with the Friday or Saturday walkthrough load-restricted and
opponent-specific — checking that the strength work and the first hard team practice of
mini-block 2 are separated by at least a full day, per the 28-30 hour figure.

**Related** — [[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],
[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]],
[[heuristic--two-a-day-workout-sequencing-by-dominant-ability]],
[[claim--morning-resistance-training-no-decrement-after-6hr-rest]],
[[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]].

specialized workloads within **mini-blocks**, separating mini-blocks by training modality, and
determining **key-workouts** within each mini-block. The worked example (Figure 3.8, PDF p.

Monday with an active-recovery session (medium/low load, aerobic and general conditioning),
then delivers the strength emphasis across **two key-workouts**, combined with a medium-load
team practice (Tuesday afternoon) and a conditioning-restorative workout (Wednesday afternoon).

mini-block 2 begins, to let the anabolic/restorative process run before the next demand.

preparation: it includes two obligatory team practices, one before the day off (intended to
deliver a pronounced game-specific stimulus) and a second, load-restricted session immediately
before the game itself (mostly techno-tactical drills tied to the specific forthcoming
opponent). Issurin notes some highly motivated teams skip the day off and add an optional
Friday-morning conditioning or techno-tactical session instead, trading recovery time for
extra preparation; he states the tradeoff explicitly without endorsing either choice. The
chart gives priority to maximal-strength development over explosive-type work within the week,
which Issurin explains as protecting "somatic, functional and anabolic status," while noting a
cited counter-example (Newton et al., 2006) of sequencing classic high-resistance training with
ballistic explosive-type mesocycles to enhance jump performance instead.

stated in [[principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]] (BPC needs concentrated,
sequenced blocks) meeting the constraint that team sports cannot suspend competition long

normally require in duration). Splitting the week itself into two purpose-specific mini-blocks,

benefit even though the underlying block can only be one week long, not several.

strength-and-conditioning miss-log's "peaking phase structure for collegiate football" gap
(logged 2026-09-03)** — Issurin explicitly names American football as a sport this structure
is meant for. **Eric's baseline's** in-season rule, "maintain intensity, reduce volume"
(`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md`

14	# Build a Microcycle Key-Workouts First: A Six-Step Sequence and Five Design Rules
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin gives a six-step operational sequence for compiling a training
17	microcycle (Table 3.6, PDF p. 112, printed p. 101): (1) determine dominant and secondary
18	training modalities, based on the annual plan and the current mesocycle's specificity; (2)
19	determine, place and compile **key-workouts** (see
20	[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]) — these carry the main development
21	impact; (3) determine restorative workouts and restorative "windows," to facilitate the
22	key-workouts and prevent excess fatigue; (4) determine, place and compile other
23	developmental/supportive workouts, paying special attention to how preceding workouts affect
24	sensitivity to subsequent ones; (5) select monitoring means for the targeted abilities and
25	functions; (6) plan special events (psychologist, physician, team meeting, etc.). Alongside
26	this sequence, Issurin states five general design rules (PDF pp. 112-113, printed pp.
27	101-102): **first**, key-workout priority — once targeted abilities are defined, design should
28	start from the key-workouts, not fill them in last; **second**, arrangement around
29	key-workouts — the preceding session affects the athlete's sensitivity to the key-workout's
30	stimulus, while the following session determines fatigue accumulation and restoration, so both
31	neighbors must be chosen deliberately; **third**, sharing restorative means — restorative
32	workouts, restorative exercises (low-intensity aerobic work, stretching, relaxation, shaking,
33	breathing) and restorative procedures (massage, sauna, hydro/physiotherapy, mental training)
34	are "indispensable" and must be expertly planned into every microcycle, not treated as
35	optional filler; **fourth**, workload initiation and peaks — a day off lowers readiness for
36	high workloads, so the first session after a day off should **not** be a key-workout; the
37	number and placement of key-workouts is what determines whether the week is a one-, two-, or
38	three-peak design (see [[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]); **fifth**,
39	monitoring — key-workout execution data (achievement level, technical quality, HR, blood
40	lactate, RPE) is the single best indicator of an athlete's current state.
41	
42	**Why it works** — This is a process heuristic, not a physiological mechanism: Issurin's
43	stated rationale is that once the microcycle's actual development stimulus (the key-workouts)

# Build a Microcycle Key-Workouts First: A Six-Step Sequence and Five Design Rules

**What it is** — Issurin gives a six-step operational sequence for compiling a training
microcycle (Table 3.6, PDF p. 112, printed p. 101): (1) determine dominant and secondary
training modalities, based on the annual plan and the current mesocycle's specificity; (2)
determine, place and compile **key-workouts** (see
[[framework--key-workout-and-key-exercise-concept]]) — these carry the main development
impact; (3) determine restorative workouts and restorative "windows," to facilitate the
key-workouts and prevent excess fatigue; (4) determine, place and compile other
developmental/supportive workouts, paying special attention to how preceding workouts affect
sensitivity to subsequent ones; (5) select monitoring means for the targeted abilities and
functions; (6) plan special events (psychologist, physician, team meeting, etc.). Alongside
this sequence, Issurin states five general design rules (PDF pp. 112-113, printed pp.
101-102): **first**, key-workout priority — once targeted abilities are defined, design should
start from the key-workouts, not fill them in last; **second**, arrangement around
key-workouts — the preceding session affects the athlete's sensitivity to the key-workout's
stimulus, while the following session determines fatigue accumulation and restoration, so both
neighbors must be chosen deliberately; **third**, sharing restorative means — restorative
workouts, restorative exercises (low-intensity aerobic work, stretching, relaxation, shaking,
breathing) and restorative procedures (massage, sauna, hydro/physiotherapy, mental training)
are "indispensable" and must be expertly planned into every microcycle, not treated as
optional filler; **fourth**, workload initiation and peaks — a day off lowers readiness for
high workloads, so the first session after a day off should **not** be a key-workout; the
number and placement of key-workouts is what determines whether the week is a one-, two-, or
three-peak design (see [[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]]); **fifth**,
monitoring — key-workout execution data (achievement level, technical quality, HR, blood
lactate, RPE) is the single best indicator of an athlete's current state.

**Why it works** — This is a process heuristic, not a physiological mechanism: Issurin's
stated rationale is that once the microcycle's actual development stimulus (the key-workouts)
is fixed, every other design decision (what precedes it, what follows it, how restoration is
distributed) exists to protect that stimulus's quality and manage the fatigue it produces —
designing "everything else first, then slotting in the hard part" risks the key-workout landing
on a fatigued or under-prepared athlete.

**When to apply** — As a checklist when building or auditing any microcycle: has the dominant
modality been named before workouts were scheduled; are the key-workouts placed away from the
first session after a day off; is there a planned restorative window around each key-workout;
and is monitoring tied specifically to key-workout performance rather than spread evenly across
every session. Useful as a coach-facing planning template independent of sport.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — This is Issurin's own applied synthesis of BPC design
logic; no citation or comparative study is given for the six-step sequence or the five rules
themselves — treat them as a structured practitioner heuristic, not an experimentally
validated planning method. **Inference:** the sequence assumes a coach already has a clear
single dominant-and-secondary modality assignment for the week (step 1); it gives no guidance
for a team-sport week that must simultaneously serve several position groups with different
dominant needs on the same day, a common real constraint in football that this chapter's
narrower single-athlete/single-event examples elsewhere do not have to solve.

**Example** — Before finalizing a week's training plan, a coach could walk the six steps in
order: name this week's dominant ability, place its key-workouts (never as the first session

eye to how each affects the next, pick 2-3 monitoring indicators tied to the key-workouts, and
only then schedule any non-training events.

[[framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]],

# Accumulation Mesocycle: 3-6 Weeks Early, Down to 10-14 Days Late-Season, With Diminishing Weekly Returns

**What it is** — This is the full prescriptive detail behind the accumulation block first
introduced conceptually in [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]
(Ch. 1). Issurin gives duration as a function of two competing factors (PDF pp. 113-115,
printed pp. 102-104): the time needed for a real cumulative training effect in the targeted
basic abilities (aerobic endurance, maximal strength — both requiring "profound morphological
and even organic changes"), versus the time limit the competition calendar allows. He cites a
supporting case study: eight highly qualified female kayakers, monitored over a **20-week**
program of high-resistance training (**4-5 hr/week**) aimed at maximal strength and aerobic
endurance, tracked via maximal isometric force in kayak-specific positions (Figure 3.9, PDF p.
114, printed p. 103, based on Sharobajko, 1984). Strength gain and weekly improvement rate fell
sharply over time: the first 3 weeks produced a 5.9% average gain (1.93%/week improvement
rate); the next 3 weeks added only 1.6% more (0.53%/week); the remaining 14 weeks added only
0.25% and then 0.13% per week. Issurin's stated conclusion: the fitness program was "very
effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six weeks, and had only a
minor effect for the next 14 weeks" — directly supporting BPC's case for shorter, higher-turnover
blocks over long, continuous ones (citing the same general adaptive-decline concept in
Bouchard, 1986, as applying to aerobic-endurance programs too). Based on this, Issurin sets the
following duration bands (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104): **up to six weeks** when deeper
physiological change is the goal (typically early season, when athletes are less
calendar-constrained); **three-four weeks** at mid-season, once important-competition timing
starts to dictate mesocycle sequencing; **10-14 days** at season's end, when important
competitions come at short intervals. Content is structured by sequencing microcycle types
(Table 3.7, PDF p. 116, printed p. 105): the **initial** part uses a restoration microcycle
(if starting a new training stage, not needed after a transition period) followed by an
adjustment microcycle (can be shorter than a week); the **mid-and-end** part is built from
loading microcycles, whose count sets the mesocycle's total length, with optional impact and/or
restoration microcycles inserted (a restorative microcycle, usually 3-6 days, can go
mid-mesocycle, or immediately after an impact microcycle before the next loading microcycle).
General load-shape rule: increase load gradually at the start, hold maximal load in the middle,
and reduce load at the end so the next mesocycle (transmutation) begins without excess fatigue;
a 3-4 day restorative microcycle can be inserted near the end of accumulation for this purpose.
Monitoring (Table 3.8, PDF p. 117, printed p. 106; verified against page image) tracks three
categories: **workload performance** (total weekly mileage, total sport-specific reps/week,
key-workout outcomes — each compared actual-vs-planned, week-to-week, and across the season);
**targeted (basic) abilities** (time-trial results, free-weight-trial results, average
key-workout results, using "appropriate valid tests"); and **training responses** (resting
heart rate, blood urea and CPK, body mass/muscle mass/fat component, blood lactate after
trials). Anthropometric change is flagged as a specific, useful side-outcome to track (strength
training raises muscle mass; aerobic training reduces fat component), especially relevant in
weight-category or leanness-sensitive sports.

**Why it works** — The kayaker case study is offered as direct evidence for the general
biological principle that "the adaptive response induced by long-term training declines with
time" (Bouchard, 1986) — i.e., diminishing returns set in within weeks, not months, for a fixed
training emphasis, which is the physiological argument for keeping each mesocycle-block short
and switching emphasis rather than running one long undifferentiated program.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — **Fall camp** functions
as a short accumulation mesocycle at the low end of Issurin's range (closer to the 10-14 day
figure, or the 3-4 week figure if camp's aerobic/strength-base emphasis is counted from
voluntary summer conditioning): given the diminishing-returns pattern in the kayaker case
(most of a strength/aerobic gain arrives in the first 3-6 weeks), a multi-month, undifferentiated
summer conditioning block is exactly the pattern this framework argues against — a shorter,
concentrated base-building window, followed by a shift to more specific work, is the BPC
alternative. **The gap between the last regular-season/conference-championship game and a bowl
game** (commonly roughly 3-5 weeks for many programs) is long enough to support a short
accumulation mesocycle (10-14 to 20-25 days, matching both this section's end-of-season figure
and the mini-block interval used later in [[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]])
if the goal is to rebuild any basic-ability deterioration accumulated over a long season before
shifting into a bowl-specific transmutation/realization sequence.

**When NOT to apply — mandatory** — The kayaker case study is a single unpublished thesis
(Sharobajko, 1984, a Ph.D. dissertation, Moscow All-Union Research Sport Institute), n = 8,
female kayakers, with no control group not receiving the same 20-week program — it demonstrates
a within-group improvement-rate curve, not a controlled comparison against an alternative
mesocycle length. **Population caveat:** this is Issurin's own book-wide pattern — the
accumulation-duration guidance and its supporting evidence are drawn from individual/endurance
Olympic sports (kayaking) tracking isometric strength and presumably aerobic markers, not from
any team-contact-sport population; football's basic-ability profile (short-duration high-force
efforts, position-specific demands, large roster with heterogeneous training age) is not
represented in this evidence base at all. The specific duration bands (six weeks / 3-4 weeks /
10-14 days) are Issurin's own applied judgment, not derived from a stated formula connecting
them to the kayaker data's exact decay curve.

**Example** — A 3-4 week early-summer strength-aerobic emphasis block, monitored against
Table 3.8's indicators (weekly key-lift totals, a repeated time-trial or aerobic test, resting
HR trend, body composition), gives a coach a citable structure for when to expect most of a
block's gain to already have happened (roughly the first half of the block, per the kayaker
curve) and when continuing the same emphasis is likely yielding only marginal further return.

[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]],
[[framework--transmutation-mesocycle-duration-and-overtraining-monitoring]],

# Accumulation Mesocycle: 3-6 Weeks Early, Down to 10-14 Days Late-Season, With Diminishing Weekly Returns

**What it is** — This is the full prescriptive detail behind the accumulation block first
introduced conceptually in [[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]]
(Ch. 1). Issurin gives duration as a function of two competing factors (PDF pp. 113-115,
printed pp. 102-104): the time needed for a real cumulative training effect in the targeted
basic abilities, aerobic endurance and maximal strength, both requiring "profound morphological
and even organic changes," versus the time limit the competition calendar allows. He cites a
supporting case study: eight highly qualified female kayakers, monitored over a **20-week**
program of high-resistance training (**4-5 hr/week**) aimed at maximal strength and aerobic
endurance, tracked via maximal isometric force in kayak-specific positions (Figure 3.9, PDF p.
114, printed p. 103, based on Sharobajko, 1984). Strength gain and weekly improvement rate fell
sharply over time: the first 3 weeks produced a 5.9% average gain (1.93%/week improvement
rate); the next 3 weeks added only 1.6% more (0.53%/week); the remaining 14 weeks added only
0.25% and then 0.13% per week. Issurin's stated conclusion: the fitness program was "very
effective at the beginning, reasonably effective through the first six weeks, and had only a
minor effect for the next 14 weeks" — directly supporting BPC's case for shorter, higher-turnover
blocks over long, continuous ones (citing the same general adaptive-decline concept in
Bouchard, 1986, as applying to aerobic-endurance programs too). Based on this, Issurin sets the
following duration bands (PDF p. 115, printed p. 104): **up to six weeks** when deeper
physiological change is the goal (typically early season, when athletes are less
calendar-constrained); **three-four weeks** at mid-season, once important-competition timing
starts to dictate mesocycle sequencing; **10-14 days** at season's end, when important
competitions come at short intervals. Content is structured by sequencing microcycle types
(Table 3.7, PDF p. 116, printed p. 105): the **initial** part uses a restoration microcycle
(if starting a new training stage, not needed after a transition period) followed by an
adjustment microcycle (can be shorter than a week); the **mid-and-end** part is built from
loading microcycles, whose count sets the mesocycle's total length, with optional impact and/or
restoration microcycles inserted (a restorative microcycle, usually 3-6 days, can go
mid-mesocycle, or immediately after an impact microcycle before the next loading microcycle).
General load-shape rule: increase load gradually at the start, hold maximal load in the middle,
and reduce load at the end so the next mesocycle (transmutation) begins without excess fatigue;
a 3-4 day restorative microcycle can be inserted near the end of accumulation for this purpose.

categories: **workload performance** (total weekly mileage, total sport-specific reps/week,
key-workout outcomes — each compared actual-vs-planned, week-to-week, and across the season);
**targeted (basic) abilities** (time-trial results, free-weight-trial results, average
key-workout results, using "appropriate valid tests"); and **training responses** (resting
heart rate, blood urea and CPK, body mass/muscle mass/fat component, blood lactate after
trials). Anthropometric change is flagged as a specific, useful side-outcome to track (strength
training raises muscle mass; aerobic training reduces fat component), especially relevant in
weight-category or leanness-sensitive sports.

biological principle that "the adaptive response induced by long-term training declines with
time" (Bouchard, 1986) — i.e., diminishing returns set in within weeks, not months, for a fixed

summer conditioning block is exactly the pattern this framework argues against — a shorter,
